The training fit is numerically consistent across the two implementations. As shown in @tbl-zip-convergence-r and @tbl-zip-convergence-py, both optimizers report convergence, all reported standard errors are finite, and the model contains **`r fmt_sig(zip_convergence_r$number_of_parameters)`** estimated parameters. The `R` maximized log-likelihood is **`r fmt_sig(zip_convergence_r$log_likelihood)`**, and the `Python` value agrees to the displayed precision. The coefficient estimates in @tbl-zip-fit-r and @tbl-zip-fit-py likewise agree closely in sign and magnitude. These checks support moving to the training-stage diagnostics, but convergence and cross-language agreement alone do not establish that the fitted ZIP distribution adequately represents the data.

::::: Tip
::: Tip-header
Tip on optimization methods for ZIP regression in `R` and `Python`
:::

::: Tip-container
ZIP likelihoods are smooth but can be numerically difficult because every observed zero couples the zero-inflation and count parameters. Different optimization algorithms search the same likelihood surface in different ways.

**In `R`:** `pscl::zeroinfl()` maximizes the likelihood through `optim()`. Its default method is **BFGS**, a quasi-Newton method that uses gradients and updates an approximation to the inverse Hessian. `zeroinfl()` can also pass another `optim()` method through `zeroinfl.control()`. For example, **Nelder--Mead** is derivative-free and can be useful as a slower fallback, while **CG** uses conjugate-gradient search directions. The package can use an **EM algorithm to construct starting values**, but the documented `zeroinfl()` implementation then performs the final maximum-likelihood optimization through `optim()` [@jackman2024pscl; @fletcher1987]. See the [`zeroinfl.control()` documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/pscl/help/zeroinfl.control.html) for the available controls.

**In `Python`:** `statsmodels.discrete.count_model.ZeroInflatedPoisson.fit()` uses **BFGS** by default and also supports methods including Newton--Raphson, Nelder--Mead, L-BFGS, Powell, conjugate gradient, Newton-conjugate gradient, and SciPy's generic `minimize()` interface. **L-BFGS** is a memory-reduced quasi-Newton method, **Newton** methods use explicit curvature and can be fast near a well-behaved optimum, and **Powell** or **Nelder--Mead** do not require gradients but can require more function evaluations [@statsmodels; @scipy]. See the [`statsmodels` ZIP fitting documentation](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.discrete.count_model.ZeroInflatedPoisson.fit.html) for the current solver list.

The optimizer should not be selected by whichever method produces the preferred coefficient signs. A reasonable workflow is to use a documented default, inspect convergence and standard errors, and then use one or two alternative methods or starting values as a sensitivity check when the fit appears unstable.
:::
:::::

::::: Tip
::: Tip-header
Tip on how the software obtains the reported standard errors
:::

::: Tip-container
Both fits report model-based standard errors derived from the curvature of the joint ZIP likelihood. In `R`, the complete covariance matrix is available through

``` r
zip_vcov_r <- vcov(zip_model_r)
zip_se_r <- sqrt(diag(zip_vcov_r))
```

The `pscl` documentation states that these standard errors are obtained numerically from the Hessian returned by `optim()` [@jackman2024pscl].

In `Python`, the same quantities are available through

``` python
zip_vcov_py = zip_result_py.cov_params()
zip_se_py = zip_result_py.bse
```

By default, `statsmodels` calculates an inverse-Hessian covariance matrix after likelihood optimization unless Hessian calculation is explicitly skipped. These standard errors are joint: the covariance matrix contains both zero-inflation and count parameters rather than treating the two blocks as unrelated regressions [@statsmodels].

Finite standard errors do not prove that the model is well identified. Very large standard errors, a nearly singular covariance matrix, or strong sensitivity to the optimizer can indicate that the data do not distinguish the two components clearly enough.
:::
:::::

This section has fitted the working ZIP model and verified its basic numerical completion. The next sections should assess whether the fitted distribution represents the training data adequately before making final component-level or marginal interpretations.


## Goodness of Fit and Diagnostics {#sec-zip-goodness-of-fit}

The ZIP model has now been fitted on the canonical training data. Successful numerical optimization is necessary, but it does not by itself establish that the fitted distribution represents the observed counts adequately. We therefore evaluate the complete fitted ZIP distribution before interpreting the coefficients or applying the model to the testing observations.

These diagnostics return to both inquiries introduced in @sec-zip-study-design:

- for the **inferential inquiry**, poor fit can make coefficient-level conclusions misleading;
- for the **predictive inquiry**, a model that reproduces only the average count but misses the zero frequency or positive-count distribution may assign poor probabilities to new observations.

The diagnostics in this section use the **training data** because they remain part of model development and specification assessment.

### Diagnostic targets in a ZIP model

For policyholder $i$, the fitted model provides

$$
\widehat{\pi}_i
=
\widehat{P}(S_i=1\mid\mathbf{x}_i),
$${#eq-zip-fitted-structural-zero-probability}

the fitted probability of structural-zero membership;

$$
\widehat{\lambda}_i
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y_i\mid S_i=0,\mathbf{x}_i),
$${#eq-zip-fitted-count-state-mean}

the fitted Poisson mean within the count-generating state;

$$
\widehat{\mu}_i
=
(1-\widehat{\pi}_i)\widehat{\lambda}_i,
$${#eq-zip-fitted-marginal-mean}

the fitted marginal expected number of claims; and

$$
\widehat{p}_{0,i}
=
\widehat{\pi}_i
+
(1-\widehat{\pi}_i)e^{-\widehat{\lambda}_i},
$${#eq-zip-fitted-observed-zero-probability}

the fitted probability of observing zero claims.

The structural-zero state is latent. Therefore, $\widehat{\pi}_i$ cannot be checked against an observed structural-zero label. The observable calibration target is $\widehat{p}_{0,i}$ because the dataset records whether $Y_i=0$, but not which latent mechanism generated that zero.

### Computing the fitted diagnostic quantities

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

```r
zip_training_diagnostics_r <- zip_training_r |>
  mutate(
    fitted_pi = as.numeric(
      predict(zip_model_r, type = "zero")
    ),
    fitted_lambda = as.numeric(
      predict(zip_model_r, type = "count")
    ),
    fitted_mu = as.numeric(
      predict(zip_model_r, type = "response")
    ),
    fitted_p_zero =
      fitted_pi +
      (1 - fitted_pi) * exp(-fitted_lambda),
    fitted_variance =
      (1 - fitted_pi) * fitted_lambda *
      (1 + fitted_pi * fitted_lambda),
    pearson_residual =
      (claims - fitted_mu) / sqrt(fitted_variance)
  )
```

## **`Python` Code**

```python
zip_training_diagnostics_py = zip_training_py.copy()

zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"] = zip_result_py.predict(
    which="mean"
)
zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_lambda"] = zip_result_py.predict(
    which="mean-main"
)
zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_pi"] = (
    1 - zip_result_py.predict(which="prob-main")
)
zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_p_zero"] = zip_result_py.predict(
    which="prob-zero"
)
zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_variance"] = zip_result_py.predict(
    which="var"
)
zip_training_diagnostics_py["pearson_residual"] = (
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["claims"]
    - zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"]
) / np.sqrt(
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_variance"]
)
```
:::

The fitted variance follows @eq-zip-marginal-variance. The `R` prediction types follow the `pscl::predict.zeroinfl()` interface, while the Python predictions use the `which` options provided by `statsmodels` [@jackman2024pscl; @statsmodels].

These fitted quantities are the inputs for the calibration, count-frequency, residual, and relative-fit diagnostics below.

```{r}
#| label: zip-gof-compute-r
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if (exists("zip_model_r") && exists("zip_training_r")) {
  zip_training_diagnostics_r <- zip_training_r |>
    mutate(
      fitted_pi = as.numeric(
        predict(zip_model_r, type = "zero")
      ),
      fitted_lambda = as.numeric(
        predict(zip_model_r, type = "count")
      ),
      fitted_mu = as.numeric(
        predict(zip_model_r, type = "response")
      ),
      fitted_p_zero =
        fitted_pi +
        (1 - fitted_pi) * exp(-fitted_lambda),
      fitted_variance =
        (1 - fitted_pi) * fitted_lambda *
        (1 + fitted_pi * fitted_lambda),
      pearson_residual =
        (claims - fitted_mu) / sqrt(fitted_variance)
    )

  zip_gof_summary_r <- tibble(
    diagnostic = c(
      "Mean claim count",
      "Zero-claim rate"
    ),
    observed = c(
      mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$claims),
      mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$claims == 0)
    ),
    fitted = c(
      mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$fitted_mu),
      mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$fitted_p_zero)
    ),
    observed_minus_fitted = observed - fitted
  )

  zip_mean_calibration_r <- zip_training_diagnostics_r |>
    mutate(
      calibration_group = dplyr::ntile(fitted_mu, 10)
    ) |>
    group_by(calibration_group) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      observed_mean = mean(claims),
      fitted_mean = mean(fitted_mu),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  zip_zero_calibration_r <- zip_training_diagnostics_r |>
    mutate(
      calibration_group = dplyr::ntile(fitted_p_zero, 10)
    ) |>
    group_by(calibration_group) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      observed_zero_rate = mean(claims == 0),
      fitted_zero_probability = mean(fitted_p_zero),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  zip_count_grid_r <- 0:max(zip_training_r$claims)

  zip_probability_matrix_r <- predict(
    zip_model_r,
    type = "prob",
    at = zip_count_grid_r
  )

  zip_count_fit_r <- tibble(
    claims = zip_count_grid_r,
    observed = vapply(
      zip_count_grid_r,
      \(count_value) sum(zip_training_r$claims == count_value),
      numeric(1)
    ),
    expected = colSums(zip_probability_matrix_r)
  )


}
```

```{python}
#| label: zip-gof-compute-py
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if "zip_result_py" in globals() and "zip_training_py" in globals():
    zip_training_diagnostics_py = zip_training_py.copy()

    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"] = zip_result_py.predict(
        which="mean"
    )
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_lambda"] = zip_result_py.predict(
        which="mean-main"
    )
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_pi"] = (
        1 - zip_result_py.predict(which="prob-main")
    )
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_p_zero"] = zip_result_py.predict(
        which="prob-zero"
    )
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_variance"] = zip_result_py.predict(
        which="var"
    )
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["pearson_residual"] = (
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["claims"]
        - zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"]
    ) / np.sqrt(
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_variance"]
    )

    zip_gof_summary_py = pd.DataFrame({
        "diagnostic": [
            "Mean claim count",
            "Zero-claim rate",
        ],
        "observed": [
            zip_training_diagnostics_py["claims"].mean(),
            (zip_training_diagnostics_py["claims"] == 0).mean(),
        ],
        "fitted": [
            zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"].mean(),
            zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_p_zero"].mean(),
        ],
    })
    zip_gof_summary_py["observed_minus_fitted"] = (
        zip_gof_summary_py["observed"]
        - zip_gof_summary_py["fitted"]
    )

    zip_training_diagnostics_py["mean_group"] = pd.qcut(
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"],
        q=10,
        duplicates="drop",
    )
    zip_mean_calibration_py = (
        zip_training_diagnostics_py
        .groupby("mean_group", observed=False)
        .agg(
            n=("claims", "size"),
            observed_mean=("claims", "mean"),
            fitted_mean=("fitted_mu", "mean"),
        )
        .reset_index()
    )

    zip_training_diagnostics_py["zero_group"] = pd.qcut(
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_p_zero"],
        q=10,
        duplicates="drop",
    )
    zip_zero_calibration_py = (
        zip_training_diagnostics_py
        .groupby("zero_group", observed=False)
        .agg(
            n=("claims", "size"),
            observed_zero_rate=(
                "claims",
                lambda values: (values == 0).mean(),
            ),
            fitted_zero_probability=("fitted_p_zero", "mean"),
        )
        .reset_index()
    )

    zip_count_grid_py = np.arange(
        0,
        int(zip_training_py["claims"].max()) + 1,
    )
    zip_probability_matrix_py = np.asarray(
        zip_result_py.predict(
            which="prob",
            y_values=zip_count_grid_py,
        ),
        dtype=float,
    )
    zip_count_fit_py = pd.DataFrame({
        "claims": zip_count_grid_py,
        "observed": [
            int((zip_training_py["claims"] == value).sum())
            for value in zip_count_grid_py
        ],
        "expected": zip_probability_matrix_py.sum(axis=0),
    })

    
```

### Overall mean and zero-frequency check

The first check compares two coarse summaries of the observed training response with the averages implied by the fitted ZIP distribution:

- **Mean claim count:** compares the sample mean of `claims` with the average fitted marginal mean from @eq-zip-fitted-marginal-mean.
- **Zero-claim rate:** compares the observed proportion of zeros with the average fitted observed-zero probability from @eq-zip-fitted-observed-zero-probability.

Agreement here is useful, but it is only a first check. A model can reproduce these two totals while still fitting poorly within subgroups or at specific count values.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_gof_summary_r <- tibble(
  diagnostic = c(
    "Mean claim count",
    "Zero-claim rate"
  ),
  observed = c(
    mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$claims),
    mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$claims == 0)
  ),
  fitted = c(
    mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$fitted_mu),
    mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$fitted_p_zero)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    observed_minus_fitted = observed - fitted
  )
```

## **`Python` Code**

``` python
zip_gof_summary_py = pd.DataFrame({
    "diagnostic": [
        "Mean claim count",
        "Zero-claim rate",
    ],
    "observed": [
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["claims"].mean(),
        (zip_training_diagnostics_py["claims"] == 0).mean(),
    ],
    "fitted": [
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"].mean(),
        zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_p_zero"].mean(),
    ],
})

zip_gof_summary_py["observed_minus_fitted"] = (
    zip_gof_summary_py["observed"]
    - zip_gof_summary_py["fitted"]
)
```
:::

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Output**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-zip-gof-summary-r
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted training-set summaries for the ZIP model using R."

if (exists("zip_gof_summary_r")) {
  zip_gof_summary_r |>
    fmt_table() |>
    print_as_dt()
} else {
  tibble(Message = "R goodness-of-fit summaries are unavailable until the ZIP model is fitted.") |>
    print_as_dt()
}
```

## **`Python` Output**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-zip-gof-summary-py
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted training-set summaries for the ZIP model using Python."

if (reticulate::py_eval("'zip_gof_summary_py' in globals()", convert = TRUE)) {
  py_df_to_tibble("zip_gof_summary_py") |>
    fmt_table() |>
    print_as_dt()
} else {
  tibble(Message = "Python goodness-of-fit summaries are unavailable until the ZIP model is fitted.") |>
    print_as_dt()
}
```
:::

The aggregate fit in @tbl-zip-gof-summary-r and @tbl-zip-gof-summary-py is very close. The observed training-set mean is **`r fmt_sig(zip_gof_summary_r$observed[zip_gof_summary_r$diagnostic == "Mean claim count"])`** claims, compared with an average fitted marginal mean of **`r fmt_sig(zip_gof_summary_r$fitted[zip_gof_summary_r$diagnostic == "Mean claim count"])`**, an absolute difference of only **`r fmt_sig(abs(zip_gof_summary_r$observed_minus_fitted[zip_gof_summary_r$diagnostic == "Mean claim count"]))`** claims. The observed zero-claim rate is **`r scales::percent(zip_gof_summary_r$observed[zip_gof_summary_r$diagnostic == "Zero-claim rate"], accuracy = 0.1)`**, while the average fitted probability of an observed zero is **`r scales::percent(zip_gof_summary_r$fitted[zip_gof_summary_r$diagnostic == "Zero-claim rate"], accuracy = 0.1)`**. Their absolute difference is about **`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * abs(zip_gof_summary_r$observed_minus_fitted[zip_gof_summary_r$diagnostic == "Zero-claim rate"]))` percentage points**. Neither aggregate discrepancy is substantively large in this training sample. However, agreement in these two totals does not show whether the model is calibrated across different fitted-risk regions or whether it reproduces the complete count distribution.

### Calibration of the marginal expected count

The overall mean can hide systematic errors across policyholder profiles. We therefore group observations by $\widehat{\mu}_i$ and compare the observed and fitted mean claim count within each group.

The code below divides the training observations into ten groups according to their fitted marginal mean. Within each group, we compare the average fitted value with the average observed count. A well-calibrated model should place the grouped points reasonably close to the 45-degree reference line, without a systematic pattern of points remaining mostly above or below it.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_mean_calibration_r <- zip_training_diagnostics_r |>
  mutate(
    calibration_group = dplyr::ntile(fitted_mu, 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(calibration_group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    observed_mean = mean(claims),
    fitted_mean = mean(fitted_mu),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  zip_mean_calibration_r,
  aes(x = fitted_mean, y = observed_mean)
) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean fitted marginal count",
    y = "Observed mean count"
  ) +
  zip_theme
```

## **`Python` Code**

``` python
zip_training_diagnostics_py["mean_group"] = pd.qcut(
    zip_training_diagnostics_py["fitted_mu"],
    q=10,
    duplicates="drop",
)

zip_mean_calibration_py = (
    zip_training_diagnostics_py
    .groupby("mean_group", observed=False)
    .agg(
        n=("claims", "size"),
        observed_mean=("claims", "mean"),
        fitted_mean=("fitted_mu", "mean"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=ZIP_FIGSIZE)

calibration_min = min(
    zip_mean_calibration_py["fitted_mean"].min(),
    zip_mean_calibration_py["observed_mean"].min(),
)
calibration_max = max(
    zip_mean_calibration_py["fitted_mean"].max(),
    zip_mean_calibration_py["observed_mean"].max(),
)

ax.plot(
    [calibration_min, calibration_max],
    [calibration_min, calibration_max],
    linestyle="--",
)

ax.scatter(
    zip_mean_calibration_py["fitted_mean"],
    zip_mean_calibration_py["observed_mean"],
    s=45,
)

ax.set_xlabel("Mean fitted marginal count")
ax.set_ylabel("Observed mean count")
zip_clean_axis(ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The grouped points in @fig-zip-mean-calibration-r and @fig-zip-mean-calibration-py remain reasonably close to the 45-degree line, so there is no broad failure of marginal-mean calibration. The deviations are local rather than uniformly in one direction: the model tends to overpredict the observed mean in some lower-middle groups, underpredict through several middle-to-upper groups, and then slightly overpredict again in the highest fitted-mean group. The largest absolute discrepancy occurs in calibration group **`r zip_mean_calibration_r$calibration_group[which.max(abs(zip_mean_calibration_r$observed_mean - zip_mean_calibration_r$fitted_mean))]`**, where the observed mean is **`r fmt_sig(zip_mean_calibration_r$observed_mean[which.max(abs(zip_mean_calibration_r$observed_mean - zip_mean_calibration_r$fitted_mean))])`** claims and the fitted mean is **`r fmt_sig(zip_mean_calibration_r$fitted_mean[which.max(abs(zip_mean_calibration_r$observed_mean - zip_mean_calibration_r$fitted_mean))])`**. The resulting gap of about **`r fmt_sig(max(abs(zip_mean_calibration_r$observed_mean - zip_mean_calibration_r$fitted_mean)))`** claims is modest relative to the fitted mean in that group, although the alternating deviations suggest that the calibration is not perfectly smooth across the fitted range.

### Calibration of the observed-zero probability

The next diagnostic groups observations by $\widehat{p}_{0,i}$ and compares the fitted zero probability with the empirical zero rate. We use $\widehat{p}_{0,i}$ rather than $\widehat{\pi}_i$ because only the observed event $Y_i=0$ can be checked directly.

Here the observable event is whether `claims == 0`. We therefore group policyholders by the fitted probability $\widehat{p}_{0,i}$ from @eq-zip-fitted-observed-zero-probability and compare that probability with the empirical zero rate in each group.

The distinction between $\widehat{\pi}_i$ and $\widehat{p}_{0,i}$ matters. Structural-zero membership is latent and cannot be checked directly from the observed response. The event $Y_i=0$, in contrast, is observed.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_zero_calibration_r <- zip_training_diagnostics_r |>
  mutate(
    calibration_group = dplyr::ntile(fitted_p_zero, 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(calibration_group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    observed_zero_rate = mean(claims == 0),
    fitted_zero_probability = mean(fitted_p_zero),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  zip_zero_calibration_r,
  aes(
    x = fitted_zero_probability,
    y = observed_zero_rate
  )
) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"

  geom_point(size = 2.5) +

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean fitted probability of an observed zero",
    y = "Observed zero rate"
  ) +
  zip_theme
```

The zero-probability calibration in @fig-zip-zero-calibration-r and @fig-zip-zero-calibration-py is also broadly close to the 45-degree line, particularly in the higher fitted-zero-probability groups. The lower and middle portions show somewhat more movement around the reference line, with both underprediction and overprediction rather than a single directional bias. The largest absolute discrepancy occurs in calibration group **`r zip_zero_calibration_r$calibration_group[which.max(abs(zip_zero_calibration_r$observed_zero_rate - zip_zero_calibration_r$fitted_zero_probability))]`**: the observed zero rate is **`r scales::percent(zip_zero_calibration_r$observed_zero_rate[which.max(abs(zip_zero_calibration_r$observed_zero_rate - zip_zero_calibration_r$fitted_zero_probability))], accuracy = 0.1)`**, compared with an average fitted zero probability of **`r scales::percent(zip_zero_calibration_r$fitted_zero_probability[which.max(abs(zip_zero_calibration_r$observed_zero_rate - zip_zero_calibration_r$fitted_zero_probability))], accuracy = 0.1)`**. The absolute gap is therefore about **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(abs(zip_zero_calibration_r$observed_zero_rate - zip_zero_calibration_r$fitted_zero_probability)))` percentage points**. Thus, the almost exact agreement in the overall zero rate does not translate into perfect group-level calibration, but the departures are local rather than evidence of a systematic failure across the full probability range.

### Observed versus fitted count frequencies

For count value $k$, define the observed frequency

$$
O_k
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\mathbb{I}(Y_i=k)
$${#eq-zip-observed-count-frequency}

and the fitted expected frequency

$$
E_k
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\widehat{P}(Y_i=k\mid\mathbf{x}_i).
$${#eq-zip-expected-count-frequency}

The comparison is distributional rather than only mean-based. It asks whether the fitted ZIP model assigns the right amount of probability mass to zero, to the common positive counts, and to the upper tail.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_count_grid_r <- 0:max(zip_training_r$claims)

zip_probability_matrix_r <- predict(
  zip_model_r,
  type = "prob",
  at = zip_count_grid_r
)

zip_count_fit_r <- tibble(
  claims = zip_count_grid_r,
  observed = vapply(
    zip_count_grid_r,
    \(count_value) sum(zip_training_r$claims == count_value),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  expected = colSums(zip_probability_matrix_r)
)

zip_count_fit_r |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(observed, expected),
    names_to = "frequency_type",
    values_to = "frequency"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    frequency_type = recode(
      frequency_type,
      observed = "Observed",
      expected = "Fitted expected"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = factor(claims),
      y = frequency,
      fill = frequency_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.75
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of claims",
    y = "Number of policyholders",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  zip_theme
```

The fitted count distribution in @fig-zip-count-frequencies-r and @fig-zip-count-frequencies-py reproduces the main shape of the training response closely. At zero claims, the model expects about **`r fmt_sig(zip_count_fit_r$expected[zip_count_fit_r$claims == 0])`** policyholders compared with **`r fmt_sig(zip_count_fit_r$observed[zip_count_fit_r$claims == 0])`** observed, so the large zero mass is represented very accurately. The largest absolute frequency discrepancy occurs at **`r zip_count_fit_r$claims[which.max(abs(zip_count_fit_r$observed - zip_count_fit_r$expected))]`** claims, with **`r fmt_sig(zip_count_fit_r$observed[which.max(abs(zip_count_fit_r$observed - zip_count_fit_r$expected))])`** observed policyholders versus **`r fmt_sig(zip_count_fit_r$expected[which.max(abs(zip_count_fit_r$observed - zip_count_fit_r$expected))])`** expected, a difference of about **`r fmt_sig(max(abs(zip_count_fit_r$observed - zip_count_fit_r$expected)))`** policyholders. The common positive counts are similarly close overall. The upper tail is less exact because very large counts are rare: the fitted model spreads a small amount of probability over some high count values with no observations, while the single observed count at the extreme of the training range is difficult to reproduce precisely. In absolute terms, however, these tail discrepancies involve very few policyholders.

### Pearson residual diagnostics

Using @eq-zip-marginal-variance, the ZIP Pearson residual is

$$
r_{P,i}
=
\frac{
y_i-\widehat{\mu}_i
}{
\sqrt{
(1-\widehat{\pi}_i)
\widehat{\lambda}_i
\left(
1+\widehat{\pi}_i\widehat{\lambda}_i
\right)
}
}.
$${#eq-zip-pearson-residual}

A residual plot against the fitted marginal mean can reveal systematic curves, changing spread, or isolated observations not explained by the fitted ZIP variance.

The residual should be interpreted against the ZIP model's own fitted marginal variance. We look primarily for:

- residuals centred around zero rather than shifted systematically upward or downward;
- no strong curved pattern in the smooth;
- no obvious increase or decrease in residual spread across the fitted-mean range;
- no small set of extreme observations dominating the plot.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
ggplot(
  zip_training_diagnostics_r,
  aes(x = fitted_mu, y = pearson_residual)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted marginal mean",
    y = "Pearson residual"
  ) +
  zip_theme
```

``` python
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.45},
    line_kws={"linewidth": 1.5},
    ax=ax,

ax.axhline(0, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Fitted marginal mean")
ax.set_ylabel("Pearson residual")

plt.show()
```

The residual pattern in @fig-zip-pearson-residuals-r and @fig-zip-pearson-residuals-py is centred close to zero overall. The mean ZIP Pearson residual is **`r fmt_sig(mean(zip_training_diagnostics_r$pearson_residual))`**, and its standard deviation is **`r fmt_sig(sd(zip_training_diagnostics_r$pearson_residual))`**. The smooth remains near zero through much of the fitted-mean range, although it drifts downward at the largest fitted means, suggesting some local overprediction in that region. A small number of observations have comparatively large residuals: **`r scales::percent(mean(abs(zip_training_diagnostics_r$pearson_residual) > 2), accuracy = 0.1)`** have absolute residuals above 2, and the largest absolute residual is **`r fmt_sig(max(abs(zip_training_diagnostics_r$pearson_residual)))`**. These observations warrant attention, but the residual cloud does not show a large global shift or a strong curvature pattern across most of the fitted range. The interpretation is based on the ZIP marginal variance in @eq-zip-pearson-residual, not on the Classical Poisson rule that variance should equal the mean.

::::: Warning
::: Warning-header
Do not reuse the Classical Poisson dispersion rule unchanged
:::

::: Warning-container
Classical Poisson regression assumes that the conditional variance equals the conditional mean. ZIP regression does not make that assumption. Its marginal variance includes the additional mixture term in @eq-zip-marginal-variance.

The relevant question is whether systematic dispersion, tail behaviour, or calibration error remains **after** accounting for the fitted ZIP distribution. A Classical Poisson Pearson dispersion statistic should not be applied into this approach and interpreted by expecting the ZIP result to be close to one.
:::
:::::


### Relative model comparison

The graphical diagnostics above ask whether the fitted ZIP distribution reproduces important features of the training data. We can complement those checks with **relative penalized-likelihood comparisons** among ZIP specifications fitted to the same response and observations.

For a model with maximized log-likelihood $\widehat{\ell}$ and $k$ estimated parameters, the Akaike Information Criterion is

$$
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\widehat{\ell}+2k,
$${#eq-zip-aic}

while the Bayesian Information Criterion is

$$
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\widehat{\ell}
+
k\log(n),
$${#eq-zip-bic}

where $n$ is the number of training observations.

For both criteria, smaller values indicate a better trade-off between fitted likelihood and model complexity. These criteria are **relative**: they tell us which of the compared specifications is preferred by the criterion, but they do not establish that any model is adequate in an absolute sense [@cameron2013countdata; @hilbe2014countdata].

Here we compare the full ZIP model with three reduced ZIP baselines.

| **Specification** | **Count component** | **Zero-inflation component** | **Interpretive purpose** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Full ZIP | All regressors | All regressors | Working specification |
| Zero-component null | All regressors | Intercept only | Asks whether the zero-component regressors improve relative fit |
| Count-component null | Intercept only | All regressors | Asks whether the count-component regressors improve relative fit |
| Complete null ZIP | Intercept only | Intercept only | Baseline with no covariate information in either ZIP mechanism |

The three reduced models are not alternative data-generating stories introduced for their own sake. They are **benchmarks inside the same ZIP family**. This makes the comparison useful for asking where the covariate information is contributing before the chapter later compares ZIP with other regression families.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_zero_null_r <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  claims ~
    driver_age_10 +
    annual_mileage_10k +
    vehicle_age_5 +
    male +
    urban_area +
    prior_claims |
    1,
  data = zip_training_r,
  dist = "poisson",
  link = "logit",
  control = pscl::zeroinfl.control(
    method = "BFGS",
    maxit = 10000,
    trace = FALSE
  )
)

zip_count_null_r <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  claims ~
    1 |
    driver_age_10 +
    annual_mileage_10k +
    vehicle_age_5 +
    male +
    urban_area +
    prior_claims,
  data = zip_training_r,
  dist = "poisson",
  link = "logit",
  control = pscl::zeroinfl.control(
    method = "BFGS",
    maxit = 10000,
    trace = FALSE
  )
)

zip_complete_null_r <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  claims ~ 1 | 1,
  data = zip_training_r,
  dist = "poisson",
  link = "logit",
  control = pscl::zeroinfl.control(
    method = "BFGS",
    maxit = 10000,
    trace = FALSE
  )
)

zip_information_criterion_row_r <- function(
  model,
  model_name,
  n_obs
) {
  model_log_likelihood <- logLik(model)

  log_likelihood <-
    as.numeric(model_log_likelihood)

  number_of_parameters <-
    attr(
      model_log_likelihood,
      "df"
    )

  tibble(
    model = model_name,
    AIC =
      -2 * log_likelihood +
      2 * number_of_parameters,
    BIC =
      -2 * log_likelihood +
      log(n_obs) *
      number_of_parameters
  )
}

zip_information_criteria_r <- bind_rows(
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_model_r,
    "Full ZIP",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  ),
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_zero_null_r,
    "Zero-component null",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  ),
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_count_null_r,
    "Count-component null",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  ),
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_complete_null_r,
    "Complete null ZIP",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    delta_AIC =
      AIC - min(AIC),
    delta_BIC =
      BIC - min(BIC)
  )
```

## **`Python` Code**

``` python

def zip_information_criterion_row(
    result,
    model_name,
    n_obs,
):

)
```

```{r}
)

zip_complete_null_r <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  claims ~ 1 | 1,
  data = zip_training_r,

  link = "logit",

    method = "BFGS",

zip_information_criterion_row_r <- function(
  model,
  model_name,
  n_obs
) {
  model_log_likelihood <- logLik(model)

  log_likelihood <-
    as.numeric(model_log_likelihood)

  number_of_parameters <-
    attr(
      model_log_likelihood,
      "df"
    )

  tibble(
    model = model_name,
    AIC =
      -2 * log_likelihood +
      2 * number_of_parameters,
    BIC =
      -2 * log_likelihood +
      log(n_obs) *
      number_of_parameters
  )
}

zip_information_criteria_r <- bind_rows(
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_model_r,
    "Full ZIP",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  ),
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_zero_null_r,
    "Zero-component null",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  ),
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_count_null_r,
    "Count-component null",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  ),
  zip_information_criterion_row_r(
    zip_complete_null_r,
    "Complete null ZIP",
    nrow(zip_training_r)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    delta_AIC =
      AIC - min(AIC),
    delta_BIC =
      BIC - min(BIC)
  )
```

The raw AIC and BIC values can be compared directly across the four ZIP specifications because all models use the same response and training observations. The `Delta AIC` and `Delta BIC` columns measure each model's difference from the smallest value of the corresponding criterion, so the criterion-preferred model has a delta of zero. To understand where the covariate information is contributing, compare each reduced model with the full ZIP specification:

- If the zero-component null has noticeably larger AIC/BIC than the full ZIP model, the zero-component regressors improve penalized fit beyond an intercept-only zero component.
- If the count-component null has noticeably larger AIC/BIC than the full ZIP model, the count-component regressors improve penalized fit beyond an intercept-only count component.
- If the complete null ZIP is clearly worse than the full ZIP model, the covariates jointly contribute useful fitted information somewhere in the ZIP structure.
- If a reduced model has the smaller criterion value, the likelihood improvement from the additional full-model regressors is not large enough, under that criterion, to offset their complexity.

AIC and BIC are not formal goodness-of-fit tests and do not replace the calibration, frequency, or residual diagnostics above.

The full ZIP specification has the smallest AIC and BIC in both @tbl-zip-information-criteria-r and @tbl-zip-information-criteria-py. Relative to the full model, the zero-component-null specification increases AIC by **`r fmt_sig(zip_information_criteria_r$delta_AIC[zip_information_criteria_r$model == "Zero-component null"])`** and BIC by **`r fmt_sig(zip_information_criteria_r$delta_BIC[zip_information_criteria_r$model == "Zero-component null"])`**, indicating that allowing the regressors to explain structural-zero membership adds substantial fitted information beyond an intercept-only zero component. The count-component-null model is even farther from the full specification, with increases of **`r fmt_sig(zip_information_criteria_r$delta_AIC[zip_information_criteria_r$model == "Count-component null"])`** in AIC and **`r fmt_sig(zip_information_criteria_r$delta_BIC[zip_information_criteria_r$model == "Count-component null"])`** in BIC, so covariate information in the count component is also important. Finally, the complete-null ZIP is worse by **`r fmt_sig(zip_information_criteria_r$delta_AIC[zip_information_criteria_r$model == "Complete null ZIP"])`** AIC units and **`r fmt_sig(zip_information_criteria_r$delta_BIC[zip_information_criteria_r$model == "Complete null ZIP"])`** BIC units. Thus, both ZIP components benefit from covariate information in the training data. These information criteria reinforce, rather than replace, the calibration, frequency, and residual diagnostics above.


### Overall adequacy conclusion

The goodness-of-fit decision should combine the evidence rather than rely on one statistic.

| **Diagnostic theme** | **Question** | **Evidence used** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Numerical stability | Was the model estimated reliably? | Convergence, finite standard errors, optimizer sensitivity |
| Marginal-mean calibration | Does the model reproduce average claim counts across fitted-risk groups? | @fig-zip-mean-calibration-r and @fig-zip-mean-calibration-py |
| Zero calibration | Does the model reproduce observed zeros across fitted-probability groups? | @fig-zip-zero-calibration-r and @fig-zip-zero-calibration-py |
| Count distribution | Does the model reproduce $0,1,2,\ldots$ claims? | @fig-zip-count-frequencies-r and @fig-zip-count-frequencies-py |
| Residual behaviour | Are systematic discrepancies still visible? | @fig-zip-pearson-residuals-r and @fig-zip-pearson-residuals-py |
| Relative fit | Do the full ZIP regressors improve penalized likelihood relative to reduced ZIP baselines? | @tbl-zip-information-criteria-r and @tbl-zip-information-criteria-py |

: Diagnostic guide for deciding whether the fitted ZIP model is adequate enough to interpret and evaluate predictively. {#tbl-zip-diagnostic-guide .striped .hover}

Taken together, the training-stage diagnostics indicate that the fitted ZIP model represents the main features of the synthetic insurance-claims distribution adequately enough to carry forward. The overall mean and zero rate are reproduced almost exactly, the grouped calibration plots show modest local departures rather than a systematic failure, and the fitted count frequencies track both the zero mass and the common positive counts closely. The Pearson residuals are centred near zero overall, although a small number of large residuals and some drift at the upper end of the fitted-mean range remain. AIC and BIC also favour the full two-component specification over each reduced ZIP baseline. The model is therefore not treated as a perfect description of every training observation, but the evidence is sufficiently coherent to freeze the specification and proceed to the testing-set refit, fitted-results interpretation, and held-out predictive assessment.

## Inference for Model Parameters {#sec-zip-parameter-inference}

The training-stage diagnostics in @sec-zip-goodness-of-fit were used to assess and freeze the working ZIP specification. We now return to the **inferential inquiry** introduced in @sec-zip-study-design:

> **How are policyholder and vehicle characteristics associated with the structural-zero probability, the count-generating mean, and the resulting marginal expected number of claims?**

For the workflow used in this chapter, the frozen ZIP specification is refitted on the testing observations. This testing-set fit supplies the coefficient estimates, standard errors, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests reported in this section. The original training estimates are retained for a split-sample comparison.

This operation is distinct from held-out prediction. The predictive section continues to use the model fitted on the training data.

### Fitting the frozen specification on the testing data

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

```r
zip_testing_r <- test_data |>
  mutate(
    driver_age_10 = driver_age / 10,
    annual_mileage_10k = annual_mileage / 10000,
    vehicle_age_5 = vehicle_age / 5
  )

zip_test_model_r <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  formula = zip_formula_r,
  data = zip_testing_r,
  dist = "poisson",
  link = "logit",
  control = pscl::zeroinfl.control(
    method = "BFGS",
    maxit = 10000,
    trace = FALSE
  )
)

summary(zip_test_model_r)
```

## **`Python` Code**

```python
zip_testing_py = testing_data.copy()

zip_testing_py["driver_age_10"] = (
    pd.to_numeric(zip_testing_py["driver_age"], errors="coerce") / 10
)
zip_testing_py["annual_mileage_10k"] = (
    pd.to_numeric(
        zip_testing_py["annual_mileage"],
        errors="coerce",
    ) / 10000
)
zip_testing_py["vehicle_age_5"] = (
    pd.to_numeric(zip_testing_py["vehicle_age"], errors="coerce") / 5
)

for column in zip_covariates_py + ["claims"]:
    zip_testing_py[column] = pd.to_numeric(
        zip_testing_py[column],
        errors="coerce",
    )

zip_testing_py = zip_testing_py.dropna(
    subset=zip_covariates_py + ["claims"]
).copy()

X_count_test_py = sm.add_constant(
    zip_testing_py[zip_covariates_py].astype(float),
    has_constant="add",
)
X_zero_test_py = X_count_test_py.copy()
y_zip_test_py = zip_testing_py["claims"].astype(int)

zip_test_model_py = ZeroInflatedPoisson(
    endog=y_zip_test_py,
    exog=X_count_test_py,
    exog_infl=X_zero_test_py,
    inflation="logit",
)

zip_test_result_py = zip_test_model_py.fit(
    method="bfgs",
    maxiter=1000,
    disp=False,
    full_output=True,
    cov_type="nonrobust",
)

print(zip_test_result_py.summary())
```
:::

The testing fit must retain the same regressors, transformations, component formulas, links, and fitting settings used for the training specification. The testing results are used to evaluate the frozen specification, not to redesign it.

The testing-set fits can now be summarized using the same coefficient and convergence structure used for the training fit.

```{r}
#| label: zip-test-model-fit-r-run
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if (exists("zip_formula_r") && exists("test_data")) {
  zip_testing_r <- test_data |>
    mutate(
      driver_age_10 = driver_age / 10,
      annual_mileage_10k = annual_mileage / 10000,
      vehicle_age_5 = vehicle_age / 5
    )

  zip_test_model_r <- pscl::zeroinfl(
    formula = zip_formula_r,
    data = zip_testing_r,
    dist = "poisson",
    link = "logit",
    control = pscl::zeroinfl.control(
      method = "BFGS",
      maxit = 10000,
      trace = FALSE
    )
  )

  zip_test_summary_r <- summary(zip_test_model_r)

  zip_test_count_coef_r <- zip_test_summary_r$coefficients$count |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
    dplyr::rename(
      estimate = Estimate,
      std_error = `Std. Error`,
      statistic = `z value`,
      p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`
    ) |>
    mutate(component = "Count", .before = 1)

  zip_test_zero_coef_r <- zip_test_summary_r$coefficients$zero |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
    dplyr::rename(
      estimate = Estimate,
      std_error = `Std. Error`,
      statistic = `z value`,
      p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`
    ) |>
    mutate(component = "Zero inflation", .before = 1)

  zip_test_coef_table_r <- bind_rows(
    zip_test_count_coef_r,
    zip_test_zero_coef_r
  )

  zip_test_se_r <- sqrt(diag(vcov(zip_test_model_r)))

  zip_test_convergence_r <- tibble(
    optimizer = zip_test_model_r$method,
    converged = zip_test_model_r$converged,
    log_likelihood = as.numeric(logLik(zip_test_model_r)),
    number_of_parameters = length(coef(zip_test_model_r)),
    finite_standard_errors = all(is.finite(zip_test_se_r))
  )
}
```

```{python}
if "testing_data" in globals() and "zip_covariates_py" in globals():
    zip_testing_py = testing_data.copy()

    zip_testing_py["driver_age_10"] = (
        pd.to_numeric(zip_testing_py["driver_age"], errors="coerce") / 10
    )
    zip_testing_py["annual_mileage_10k"] = (
        pd.to_numeric(
            zip_testing_py["annual_mileage"],
            errors="coerce",
        ) / 10000
    )
    zip_testing_py["vehicle_age_5"] = (
        pd.to_numeric(zip_testing_py["vehicle_age"], errors="coerce") / 5
    )

    for column in zip_covariates_py + ["claims"]:
        zip_testing_py[column] = pd.to_numeric(
            zip_testing_py[column],
            errors="coerce",
        )

    zip_testing_py = zip_testing_py.dropna(
        subset=zip_covariates_py + ["claims"]
    ).copy()

    X_count_test_py = sm.add_constant(
        zip_testing_py[zip_covariates_py].astype(float),
        has_constant="add",
    )
    X_zero_test_py = X_count_test_py.copy()
    y_zip_test_py = zip_testing_py["claims"].astype(int)

    zip_test_model_py = ZeroInflatedPoisson(
        endog=y_zip_test_py,
        exog=X_count_test_py,
        exog_infl=X_zero_test_py,
        inflation="logit",
    )

    zip_test_result_py = zip_test_model_py.fit(
        method="bfgs",
        maxiter=1000,
        disp=False,
        full_output=True,
        cov_type="nonrobust",
    )

    zip_test_ci_py = pd.DataFrame(
        np.asarray(zip_test_result_py.conf_int()),
        index=zip_test_result_py.params.index,
        columns=["conf_low", "conf_high"],
    )

    zip_test_coef_table_py = pd.DataFrame({
        "raw_term": zip_test_result_py.params.index,
        "estimate": zip_test_result_py.params.values,
        "std_error": zip_test_result_py.bse.values,
        "statistic": zip_test_result_py.tvalues.values,
        "p_value": zip_test_result_py.pvalues.values,
        "conf_low": zip_test_ci_py["conf_low"].values,
        "conf_high": zip_test_ci_py["conf_high"].values,
    })

    zip_test_coef_table_py["component"] = np.where(
        zip_test_coef_table_py["raw_term"].str.startswith("inflate_"),
        "Zero inflation",
        "Count",
    )
    zip_test_coef_table_py["term"] = (
        zip_test_coef_table_py["raw_term"]
        .str.replace(r"^inflate_", "", regex=True)
    )
    zip_test_coef_table_py = zip_test_coef_table_py[[
        "component",
        "term",
        "estimate",
        "std_error",
        "statistic",
        "p_value",
    ]]

    zip_test_convergence_py = pd.DataFrame({
        "optimizer": [
            zip_test_result_py.mle_settings.get("optimizer", "bfgs")
        ],
        "converged": [
            bool(zip_test_result_py.mle_retvals.get("converged", False))
        ],
        "log_likelihood": [zip_test_result_py.llf],
        "number_of_parameters": [len(zip_test_result_py.params)],
        "finite_standard_errors": [
            bool(np.isfinite(zip_test_result_py.bse).all())
        ],
    })
```

The frozen testing-set refit completed successfully in both implementations. As shown in @tbl-zip-test-convergence-r and @tbl-zip-test-convergence-py, both optimizers report convergence, all reported standard errors are finite, and both fits estimate **`r fmt_sig(zip_test_convergence_r$number_of_parameters)`** parameters. The `R` maximized log-likelihood is **`r fmt_sig(zip_test_convergence_r$log_likelihood)`**, and the `Python` result agrees to the displayed precision. There is therefore no immediate numerical warning that would prevent coefficient-level interpretation. The testing-set standard errors are nevertheless expected to be wider than the training-set standard errors because only **`r nrow(zip_testing_r)`** observations contribute to this refit, so the strength of the inferential evidence should be judged from the reported intervals and tests rather than from coefficient direction alone.

### Wald inference for individual coefficients

Let $\theta_j$ denote one coefficient from either the zero-inflation or count component. The Wald statistic is

$$
z_j
=
\frac{
\widehat{\theta}_j
}{
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat{\theta}_j)
}.
$${#eq-zip-wald-statistic}

The corresponding two-sided hypotheses are

$$
H_0:\theta_j=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_A:\theta_j\ne0.
$${#eq-zip-wald-hypotheses}

Under the usual large-sample approximation, $z_j$ is compared with a standard Normal reference distribution. A Wald confidence interval is

$$
\widehat{\theta}_j
\pm
z_{1-\alpha/2}
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat{\theta}_j).
$${#eq-zip-wald-confidence-interval}

The standard errors come from the joint testing-set covariance matrix. They should not be calculated by fitting separate Logistic and Poisson models to the two ZIP components.

### The two component hypotheses answer different questions

For regressor $x_j$, the zero-component null hypothesis is

$$
H_0:\alpha_j=0.
$${#eq-zip-zero-component-null}

This asks whether $x_j$ is associated with the log-odds of latent structural-zero membership, holding the other zero-component regressors fixed.

The count-component null hypothesis is

$$
H_0:\beta_j=0.
$${#eq-zip-count-component-null}

This asks whether $x_j$ is associated with the log mean among policyholders in the count-generating state, holding the other count-component regressors fixed.

These are **component-specific questions**. Evidence against @eq-zip-zero-component-null does not imply evidence against @eq-zip-count-component-null, and vice versa.

### Coefficient estimates, intervals, and transformed effects

The testing-set coefficient table brings together four related pieces of information for each ZIP coefficient:

- **Estimate:** the fitted change on the component's linear-predictor scale.
- **Standard Error:** the estimated sampling uncertainty of that coefficient, obtained from the joint ZIP covariance matrix.
- **95% Wald Confidence Interval:** an approximate interval on the coefficient scale.
- **Transformed Effect:** $\exp(\widehat{\alpha}_j)$ for the zero component or $\exp(\widehat{\beta}_j)$ for the count component, together with the transformed interval.

Because the continuous regressors were scaled before fitting, a one-unit comparison has a practical interpretation:

- one unit of `driver_age_10` is 10 years;
- one unit of `annual_mileage_10k` is 10,000 kilometres per year;
- one unit of `vehicle_age_5` is five years;
- a one-unit change in each binary regressor compares coding $1$ with coding $0$.

For the **zero-inflation component**, exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio for **latent structural-zero membership**. It is not an odds ratio for observing zero claims. For the **count component**, exponentiating a coefficient gives a rate ratio for the Poisson mean **within the count-generating state** [@lambert1992zip; @cameron2013countdata].

The table should therefore be read component by component first, and then connected through the joint and marginal analyses below.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_inference_table_r <- zip_test_coef_table_r |>
  mutate(
    conf_low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
    conf_high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
    transformed_effect = exp(estimate),
    transformed_low = exp(conf_low),
    transformed_high = exp(conf_high),
    effect_scale = if_else(
      component == "Zero inflation",
      "Structural-zero odds ratio",
      "Count-state rate ratio"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    component,
    term,
    estimate,
    std_error,
    statistic,
    p_value,
    conf_low,
    conf_high,
    effect_scale,
    transformed_effect,
    transformed_low,
    transformed_high
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: zip-inference-compute-r
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if (exists("zip_test_coef_table_r") && exists("zip_test_model_r")) {
  zip_inference_table_r <- zip_test_coef_table_r |>
    mutate(
      conf_low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
      conf_high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
      transformed_effect = exp(estimate),
      transformed_low = exp(conf_low),
      transformed_high = exp(conf_high),
      effect_scale = if_else(
        component == "Zero inflation",
        "Structural-zero odds ratio",
        "Count-state rate ratio"
      )
    ) |>
    select(
      component,
      term,
      estimate,
      std_error,
      statistic,
      p_value,
      conf_low,
      conf_high,
      effect_scale,
      transformed_effect,
      transformed_low,
      transformed_high
    )

  zip_test_parameters_r <- coef(zip_test_model_r)
  zip_test_vcov_r <- vcov(zip_test_model_r)

  zip_joint_terms_r <- c(
    "driver_age_10",
    "annual_mileage_10k",
    "vehicle_age_5",
    "male",
    "urban_area",
    "prior_claims"
  )

  zip_joint_wald_r <- purrr::map_dfr(
    zip_joint_terms_r,
    function(term_name) {
      coefficient_names <- c(
        paste0("zero_", term_name),
        paste0("count_", term_name)
      )

      if (!all(coefficient_names %in% names(zip_test_parameters_r))) {
        return(tibble(
          term = term_name,
          statistic = NA_real_,
          degrees_of_freedom = 2,
          p_value = NA_real_
        ))
      }

      joint_estimate <- zip_test_parameters_r[coefficient_names]
      joint_vcov <- zip_test_vcov_r[
        coefficient_names,
        coefficient_names,
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      joint_statistic <- as.numeric(
        t(joint_estimate) %*%
          solve(joint_vcov) %*%
          joint_estimate
      )

      tibble(
        term = term_name,
        statistic = joint_statistic,
        degrees_of_freedom = 2,
        p_value = pchisq(
          joint_statistic,
          df = 2,
          lower.tail = FALSE
        )
      )
    }
  )
}
```

```{python}
#| label: zip-inference-compute-py
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if "zip_test_coef_table_py" in globals() and "zip_test_result_py" in globals():
    from scipy.stats import chi2

    zip_inference_table_py = zip_test_coef_table_py.copy()
    zip_inference_table_py["conf_low"] = (
        zip_inference_table_py["estimate"]
        - 1.96 * zip_inference_table_py["std_error"]
    )
    zip_inference_table_py["conf_high"] = (
        zip_inference_table_py["estimate"]
        + 1.96 * zip_inference_table_py["std_error"]
    )
    zip_inference_table_py["transformed_effect"] = np.exp(
        zip_inference_table_py["estimate"]
    )
    zip_inference_table_py["transformed_low"] = np.exp(
        zip_inference_table_py["conf_low"]
    )
    zip_inference_table_py["transformed_high"] = np.exp(
        zip_inference_table_py["conf_high"]
    )
    zip_inference_table_py["effect_scale"] = np.where(
        zip_inference_table_py["component"] == "Zero inflation",
        "Structural-zero odds ratio",
        "Count-state rate ratio",
    )

    zip_inference_table_py = zip_inference_table_py[[
        "component",
        "term",
        "estimate",
        "std_error",
        "statistic",
        "p_value",
        "conf_low",
        "conf_high",
        "effect_scale",
        "transformed_effect",
        "transformed_low",
        "transformed_high",
    ]]

    zip_test_parameters_py = zip_test_result_py.params
    zip_test_vcov_py = zip_test_result_py.cov_params()

    zip_joint_terms_py = [
        "driver_age_10",
        "annual_mileage_10k",
        "vehicle_age_5",
        "male",
        "urban_area",
        "prior_claims",
    ]

    joint_rows_py = []

    for term_name in zip_joint_terms_py:
        coefficient_names = [
            f"inflate_{term_name}",
            term_name,
        ]

        if not all(
            name in zip_test_parameters_py.index
            for name in coefficient_names
        ):
            joint_rows_py.append({
                "term": term_name,
                "statistic": np.nan,
                "degrees_of_freedom": 2,
                "p_value": np.nan,
            })
            continue

        joint_estimate = (
            zip_test_parameters_py
            .loc[coefficient_names]
            .to_numpy()
        )
        joint_vcov = (
            zip_test_vcov_py
            .loc[coefficient_names, coefficient_names]
            .to_numpy()
        )
        joint_statistic = float(
            joint_estimate.T
            @ np.linalg.solve(joint_vcov, joint_estimate)
        )

        joint_rows_py.append({
            "term": term_name,
            "statistic": joint_statistic,
            "degrees_of_freedom": 2,
            "p_value": chi2.sf(joint_statistic, df=2),
        })

    zip_joint_wald_py = pd.DataFrame(joint_rows_py)
```

The testing-set count component in @tbl-zip-inference-r and @tbl-zip-inference-py provides the clearest evidence for annual mileage and prior claims. Holding the remaining regressors fixed, a 10,000-km increase in annual mileage multiplies the fitted count-state mean by **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_effect[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "annual_mileage_10k"])`**, with an approximate 95% Wald interval from **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_low[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "annual_mileage_10k"])`** to **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_high[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "annual_mileage_10k"])`**. Policyholders with prior claims have a fitted count-state mean multiplied by **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_effect[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "prior_claims"])`** relative to those without prior claims, with an interval from **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_low[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "prior_claims"])`** to **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_high[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "prior_claims"])`**. The `urban_area` count-state rate ratio is **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_effect[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Count" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "urban_area"])`**, with its interval remaining just above 1. By contrast, the count-component intervals for driver age, vehicle age, and the male indicator include the neutral rate ratio of 1.

The zero-inflation component tells a complementary story. A 10,000-km mileage increase multiplies the fitted **odds of structural-zero membership** by **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_effect[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Zero inflation" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "annual_mileage_10k"])`**, with a 95% interval from **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_low[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Zero inflation" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "annual_mileage_10k"])`** to **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_high[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Zero inflation" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "annual_mileage_10k"])`**. Prior claims similarly multiply the structural-zero odds by **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_effect[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Zero inflation" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "prior_claims"])`**, with an interval from **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_low[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Zero inflation" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "prior_claims"])`** to **`r fmt_sig(zip_inference_table_r$transformed_high[zip_inference_table_r$component == "Zero inflation" & zip_inference_table_r$term == "prior_claims"])`**. Both effects are below 1, associating higher mileage and prior claims with lower odds of belonging to the latent structural-zero state. The driver-age interval narrowly includes 1, while the intervals for vehicle age, the male indicator, and urban area are wider and also include 1. These zero-component odds ratios concern **latent structural-zero membership**; they are not odds ratios for the observed event `claims == 0`.

### Joint tests across both ZIP components

The component-specific tests above answer two separate questions for each regressor. Sometimes, however, the broader question is:

> **Does this regressor contribute to the ZIP model through either mechanism?**

For regressor $x_j$, the joint null is

$$
H_0:
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha_j\\
\beta_j
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
$${#eq-zip-joint-component-null}

Under this null, the regressor has no coefficient contribution in **either** ZIP component. Rejecting it means that the pair of coefficients is inconsistent with both being zero simultaneously. It does **not** tell us which component is responsible; the component-specific results must still be inspected for that interpretation.

Collect the two estimates into

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_j
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\alpha}_j\\
\widehat{\beta}_j
\end{pmatrix}.
$${#eq-zip-joint-coefficient-vector}

Let $\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\delta_j}$ be the corresponding $2\times2$ block of the full testing-set covariance matrix. The joint Wald statistic is

$$
W_j
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_j^\top
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\delta_j}^{-1}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_j.
$${#eq-zip-joint-component-wald}

The statistic measures how far the estimated coefficient pair is from the joint-null point $(0,0)$ after accounting for the pair's estimated uncertainty. The covariance term matters because $\widehat{\alpha}_j$ and $\widehat{\beta}_j$ were estimated as part of the same ZIP likelihood rather than as unrelated quantities.

Under the usual large-sample approximation, $W_j$ is compared with a Chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom [@wasserman2004; @cameron2013countdata].

::::: Tip
::: Tip-header
Tip on reading the two-component Wald test
:::

::: Tip-container
The joint test is an **omnibus test for the coefficient pair**.

- A small joint $p$-value means that the data are difficult to reconcile with $\alpha_j=\beta_j=0$ simultaneously.
- A large joint $p$-value means that the data do not provide strong evidence against that joint null.
- The test does not say that the two component effects are equal, have the same sign, or have the same practical importance.
- A regressor can have a strong effect in one component and little evidence in the other and still produce a meaningful joint result.

Geometrically, the test asks whether the uncertainty region for the pair $(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ is sufficiently far from the origin after accounting for the covariance between the two estimates. This is the multivariate extension of the one-coefficient Wald idea introduced earlier in the cookbook.
:::
:::::

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_test_parameters_r <- coef(zip_test_model_r)
zip_test_vcov_r <- vcov(zip_test_model_r)

zip_joint_terms_r <- c(
  "driver_age_10",
  "annual_mileage_10k",
  "vehicle_age_5",
  "male",
  "urban_area",
  "prior_claims"
)

zip_joint_wald_r <- purrr::map_dfr(
  zip_joint_terms_r,
  function(term_name) {
    coefficient_names <- c(
      paste0("zero_", term_name),
      paste0("count_", term_name)
    )

    joint_estimate <- zip_test_parameters_r[coefficient_names]

    joint_vcov <- zip_test_vcov_r[
      coefficient_names,
      coefficient_names,
      drop = FALSE
    ]

    joint_statistic <- as.numeric(
      t(joint_estimate) %*%
        solve(joint_vcov) %*%
        joint_estimate
    )

    tibble(
      term = term_name,
      statistic = joint_statistic,
      degrees_of_freedom = 2,
      p_value = pchisq(
        joint_statistic,
        df = 2,
        lower.tail = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
)
```

The joint tests in @tbl-zip-joint-wald-r and @tbl-zip-joint-wald-py reinforce the strongest component-specific findings. Annual mileage and prior claims both give very small joint $p$-values in `R` and `Python`, consistent with the preceding result that each regressor contributes through both the zero-inflation and count components. Driver age is weaker: the `R` joint test gives **`r sprintf("%.3f", zip_joint_wald_r$p_value[zip_joint_wald_r$term == "driver_age_10"])`**, whereas the corresponding `Python` value is slightly above 0.05. This is best treated as modest, implementation-sensitive evidence rather than as a robust two-component result. The urban-area coefficient has testing-set evidence in the count component alone, but its two-degree-of-freedom joint test is not below 0.05, illustrating that a single component-level result does not automatically imply rejection of the broader two-component null. Vehicle age and the male indicator do not show strong evidence in either component or in their joint tests.

### Comparing the training and testing estimates

The testing-set refit uses the **same frozen model specification** on a different subset of observations. The comparison below is therefore a **split-sample stability check**: it asks whether the main coefficient directions and approximate magnitudes found in training are reproduced when the same specification is estimated on the testing subset.

This is not a new model-selection step. The testing results should not be used to redesign the model and then reported as if the same testing data were still untouched.

For a common coefficient $\theta_j$, the difference between the two estimates is

$$
\widehat{\theta}_{j,\operatorname{test}}
-
\widehat{\theta}_{j,\operatorname{train}}.
$${#eq-zip-split-coefficient-raw-difference}

Because the training and testing subsets were created by a disjoint random split, the large-sample variance of this difference is approximated by the sum of the two estimated variances. The standardized difference is therefore

$$
z_{\operatorname{diff},j}
=
\frac{
\widehat{\theta}_{j,\operatorname{test}}
-
\widehat{\theta}_{j,\operatorname{train}}
}{
\sqrt{
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat{\theta}_{j,\operatorname{test}})^2
+
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat{\theta}_{j,\operatorname{train}})^2
}
}.
$${#eq-zip-split-coefficient-difference}

Values of $z_{\operatorname{diff},j}$ near zero indicate that the observed split-to-split difference is small relative to its estimated uncertainty. Large absolute values indicate a larger discrepancy relative to that uncertainty.

We can also compare the complete common parameter vector jointly:

$$
W_{\operatorname{diff}}
=
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\operatorname{test}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\operatorname{train}}
\right)^\top
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\operatorname{test}}
+
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\operatorname{train}}
\right)^{-1}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\operatorname{test}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\operatorname{train}}
\right).
$${#eq-zip-split-joint-difference}

This global statistic is an omnibus check of whether the two estimated parameter vectors differ more than would be expected from their estimated sampling uncertainty. Under strong large-sample regularity conditions, it can be compared with a Chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of common coefficients.

The coefficient-level table and the global statistic answer complementary questions. The first shows **where** discrepancies occur; the second summarizes whether the vector as a whole shows evidence of a split-to-split difference.

::: panel-tabset
## **`R` Code**

``` r
zip_training_compare_r <- zip_coef_table_r |>
  transmute(
    component,
    term,
    training_estimate = estimate,
    training_std_error = std_error,
    training_conf_low =
      estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
    training_conf_high =
      estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error
  )

zip_testing_compare_r <- zip_test_coef_table_r |>
  transmute(
    component,
    term,
    testing_estimate = estimate,
    testing_std_error = std_error,
    testing_conf_low =
      estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
    testing_conf_high =
      estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error
  )

zip_split_comparison_r <- zip_training_compare_r |>
  inner_join(
    zip_testing_compare_r,
    by = c("component", "term")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    same_direction =
      sign(training_estimate) == sign(testing_estimate),
    standardized_difference =
      (testing_estimate - training_estimate) /
      sqrt(
        training_std_error^2 +
        testing_std_error^2
      ),
    difference_p_value =
      2 * pnorm(-abs(standardized_difference))
  )

zip_train_parameters_r <- coef(zip_model_r)
zip_test_parameters_r <- coef(zip_test_model_r)

zip_common_parameters_r <- intersect(
  names(zip_train_parameters_r),
  names(zip_test_parameters_r)
)

zip_parameter_difference_r <-
  zip_test_parameters_r[zip_common_parameters_r] -
  zip_train_parameters_r[zip_common_parameters_r]

zip_difference_vcov_r <-
  vcov(zip_test_model_r)[
    zip_common_parameters_r,
    zip_common_parameters_r,
    drop = FALSE
  ] +
  vcov(zip_model_r)[
    zip_common_parameters_r,
    zip_common_parameters_r,
    drop = FALSE
  ]

zip_split_global_statistic_r <- as.numeric(
  t(zip_parameter_difference_r) %*%
    solve(zip_difference_vcov_r) %*%
    zip_parameter_difference_r
)

zip_split_global_r <- tibble(
  statistic = zip_split_global_statistic_r,
  degrees_of_freedom = length(zip_common_parameters_r),
  p_value = pchisq(
    zip_split_global_statistic_r,
    df = length(zip_common_parameters_r),
    lower.tail = FALSE
  )
)
```

``` python
from scipy.stats import chi2

zip_training_compare_py = zip_coef_table_py[[
    "component",
    "term",
    "estimate",
    "std_error",
]].copy()

zip_training_compare_py = zip_training_compare_py.rename(columns={
    "estimate": "training_estimate",
    "std_error": "training_std_error",
})

zip_training_compare_py["training_conf_low"] = (
    zip_training_compare_py["training_estimate"]
    - 1.96 * zip_training_compare_py["training_std_error"]
)

zip_training_compare_py["training_conf_high"] = (
    zip_training_compare_py["training_estimate"]
    + 1.96 * zip_training_compare_py["training_std_error"]
)

zip_testing_compare_py = zip_test_coef_table_py[[
    "component",
    "term",
    "estimate",
    "std_error",
]].copy()

zip_testing_compare_py = zip_testing_compare_py.rename(columns={
    "estimate": "testing_estimate",
    "std_error": "testing_std_error",
})

zip_testing_compare_py["testing_conf_low"] = (
    zip_testing_compare_py["testing_estimate"]
    - 1.96 * zip_testing_compare_py["testing_std_error"]
)

zip_testing_compare_py["testing_conf_high"] = (
    zip_testing_compare_py["testing_estimate"]
    + 1.96 * zip_testing_compare_py["testing_std_error"]
)

zip_split_comparison_py = zip_training_compare_py.merge(
    zip_testing_compare_py,
    on=["component", "term"],
    how="inner",
)

zip_split_comparison_py["same_direction"] = (
    np.sign(zip_split_comparison_py["training_estimate"])
    == np.sign(zip_split_comparison_py["testing_estimate"])
)

zip_split_comparison_py["standardized_difference"] = (
    zip_split_comparison_py["testing_estimate"]
    - zip_split_comparison_py["training_estimate"]
) / np.sqrt(
    zip_split_comparison_py["training_std_error"] ** 2
    + zip_split_comparison_py["testing_std_error"] ** 2
)

zip_split_comparison_py["difference_p_value"] = chi2.sf(
    zip_split_comparison_py["standardized_difference"] ** 2,
    df=1,
)

zip_common_parameters_py = [
    name
    for name in zip_result_py.params.index
    if name in zip_test_result_py.params.index
]

zip_parameter_difference_py = (
    zip_test_result_py.params.loc[zip_common_parameters_py]
    - zip_result_py.params.loc[zip_common_parameters_py]
).to_numpy()

zip_train_vcov_py = pd.DataFrame(
    zip_result_py.cov_params(),
    index=zip_result_py.params.index,
    columns=zip_result_py.params.index,
)

zip_test_vcov_py = pd.DataFrame(
    zip_test_result_py.cov_params(),
    index=zip_test_result_py.params.index,
    columns=zip_test_result_py.params.index,
)

zip_difference_vcov_py = (
    zip_test_vcov_py.loc[
        zip_common_parameters_py,
        zip_common_parameters_py,
    ].to_numpy()
    +
    zip_train_vcov_py.loc[
        zip_common_parameters_py,
        zip_common_parameters_py,
    ].to_numpy()
)

zip_split_global_statistic_py = float(
    zip_parameter_difference_py.T
    @ np.linalg.solve(
        zip_difference_vcov_py,
        zip_parameter_difference_py,
    )
)

zip_split_global_py = pd.DataFrame({
    "statistic": [zip_split_global_statistic_py],
    "degrees_of_freedom": [len(zip_common_parameters_py)],
    "p_value": [
        chi2.sf(
            zip_split_global_statistic_py,
            df=len(zip_common_parameters_py),
        )
    ],
})
```

```{r}
if (
  exists("zip_coef_table_r") &&
  exists("zip_test_coef_table_r") &&
  exists("zip_model_r") &&
  exists("zip_test_model_r")
) {
  zip_training_compare_r <- zip_coef_table_r |>
    transmute(
      component,
      term,
      training_estimate = estimate,
      training_std_error = std_error,
      training_conf_low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
      training_conf_high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error
    )

  zip_testing_compare_r <- zip_test_coef_table_r |>
    transmute(
      component,
      term,
      testing_estimate = estimate,
      testing_std_error = std_error,
      testing_conf_low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
      testing_conf_high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error
    )

  zip_split_comparison_r <- zip_training_compare_r |>
    inner_join(
      zip_testing_compare_r,
      by = c("component", "term")
    ) |>
    mutate(
      same_direction =
        sign(training_estimate) == sign(testing_estimate),
      standardized_difference =
        (testing_estimate - training_estimate) /
        sqrt(training_std_error^2 + testing_std_error^2),
      difference_p_value =
        2 * pnorm(-abs(standardized_difference))
    )

  zip_train_parameters_r <- coef(zip_model_r)
  zip_test_parameters_r <- coef(zip_test_model_r)
  zip_common_parameters_r <- intersect(
    names(zip_train_parameters_r),
    names(zip_test_parameters_r)
  )

  zip_parameter_difference_r <-
    zip_test_parameters_r[zip_common_parameters_r] -
    zip_train_parameters_r[zip_common_parameters_r]

  zip_difference_vcov_r <-
    vcov(zip_test_model_r)[
      zip_common_parameters_r,
      zip_common_parameters_r,
      drop = FALSE
    ] +
    vcov(zip_model_r)[
      zip_common_parameters_r,
      zip_common_parameters_r,
      drop = FALSE
    ]

  zip_split_global_statistic_r <- as.numeric(
    t(zip_parameter_difference_r) %*%
      solve(zip_difference_vcov_r) %*%
      zip_parameter_difference_r
  )

  zip_split_global_r <- tibble(
    statistic = zip_split_global_statistic_r,
    degrees_of_freedom = length(zip_common_parameters_r),
    p_value = pchisq(
      zip_split_global_statistic_r,
      df = length(zip_common_parameters_r),
      lower.tail = FALSE
    )
  )
}
```
