``` python
)
zip_test_lambda_py = np.asarray(
    zip_result_py.predict(
        exog=X_count_test_py,
        exog_infl=X_zero_test_py,
        which="mean-main",
    ),
    dtype=float,
)
zip_test_pi_py = 1 - np.asarray(
    zip_result_py.predict(
        exog=X_count_test_py,
        exog_infl=X_zero_test_py,
        which="prob-main",
    ),
    dtype=float,
)
zip_test_p_zero_py = np.asarray(
    zip_result_py.predict(
        exog=X_count_test_py,
        exog_infl=X_zero_test_py,
        which="prob-zero",
    ),
    dtype=float,
)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: zip-alt-prediction-compute-r
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if (
  exists("lr_model_r") &&
  exists("cpr_model_r") &&
  exists("zip_model_r") &&
  exists("test_data")
) {
  zip_alt_testing_r <- test_data |>
    mutate(
      driver_age_10 = driver_age / 10,
      annual_mileage_10k = annual_mileage / 10000,
      vehicle_age_5 = vehicle_age / 5
    )

  zip_alt_test_claims_r <- as.numeric(test_data$claims)
  zip_alt_test_zero_r <- as.integer(zip_alt_test_claims_r == 0)

  lr_test_p_claim_r <- as.numeric(
    predict(
      lr_model_r,
      newdata = test_data,
      type = "response"
    )
  )
  lr_test_p_zero_r <- 1 - lr_test_p_claim_r

  cpr_test_mu_r <- as.numeric(
    predict(
      cpr_model_r,
      newdata = test_data,
      type = "response"
    )
  )
  cpr_test_p_zero_r <- exp(-cpr_test_mu_r)

  zip_test_mu_r <- as.numeric(
    predict(
      zip_model_r,
      newdata = zip_alt_testing_r,
      type = "response"
    )
  )
  zip_test_lambda_r <- as.numeric(
    predict(
      zip_model_r,
      newdata = zip_alt_testing_r,
      type = "count"
    )
  )
  zip_test_pi_r <- as.numeric(
    predict(
      zip_model_r,
      newdata = zip_alt_testing_r,
      type = "zero"
    )
  )
  zip_test_p_zero_r <-
    zip_test_pi_r +
    (1 - zip_test_pi_r) * exp(-zip_test_lambda_r)

  zip_alt_point_metric_row_r <- function(model_name, prediction) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      mean_error = mean(zip_alt_test_claims_r - prediction),
      MAE = mean(abs(zip_alt_test_claims_r - prediction)),
      RMSE = sqrt(mean((zip_alt_test_claims_r - prediction)^2))
    )
  }

  zip_alt_point_metrics_r <- bind_rows(
    zip_alt_point_metric_row_r(
      "Classical Poisson Regression",
      cpr_test_mu_r
    ),
    zip_alt_point_metric_row_r(
      "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression",
      zip_test_mu_r
    )
  )

  zip_alt_zero_metric_row_r <- function(model_name, predicted_p_zero) {
    p <- pmin(pmax(predicted_p_zero, 1e-12), 1 - 1e-12)

    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      zero_brier_score = mean(
        (zip_alt_test_zero_r - p)^2
      ),
      zero_log_loss = -mean(
        zip_alt_test_zero_r * log(p) +
          (1 - zip_alt_test_zero_r) * log(1 - p)
      )
    )
  }

  zip_alt_zero_metrics_r <- bind_rows(
    zip_alt_zero_metric_row_r(
      "Binary Logistic Regression",
      lr_test_p_zero_r
    ),
    zip_alt_zero_metric_row_r(
      "Classical Poisson Regression",
      cpr_test_p_zero_r
    ),
    zip_alt_zero_metric_row_r(
      "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression",
      zip_test_p_zero_r
    )
  )

  cpr_observed_mass_r <- dpois(
    zip_alt_test_claims_r,
    lambda = cpr_test_mu_r
  )

  zip_observed_mass_alt_r <- ifelse(
    zip_alt_test_claims_r == 0,
    zip_test_p_zero_r,
    (1 - zip_test_pi_r) * dpois(
      zip_alt_test_claims_r,
      lambda = zip_test_lambda_r
    )
  )

  zip_alt_distribution_metrics_r <- tibble(
    model = c(
      "Classical Poisson Regression",
      "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"
    ),
    mean_negative_log_predictive_mass = c(
      mean(-log(pmax(cpr_observed_mass_r, 1e-12))),
      mean(-log(pmax(zip_observed_mass_alt_r, 1e-12)))
    )
  )

  zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r <- tibble(
    model = c(
      "Binary Logistic Regression",
      "Classical Poisson Regression",
      "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"
    )
  ) |>
    left_join(zip_alt_point_metrics_r, by = "model") |>
    left_join(zip_alt_zero_metrics_r, by = "model") |>
    left_join(zip_alt_distribution_metrics_r, by = "model")

  zip_alt_prediction_plot_r <- zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -model,
      names_to = "metric",
      values_to = "value"
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(value)) |>
    mutate(
      metric = recode(
        metric,
        mean_error = "Mean Error",
        MAE = "MAE",
        RMSE = "RMSE",
        zero_brier_score = "Zero Brier Score",
        zero_log_loss = "Zero Log Loss",
        mean_negative_log_predictive_mass =
          "Mean Negative Log Predictive Mass"
      )
    )
}
```

```{python}
#| label: zip-alt-prediction-compute-py
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

if (
    "lr_model_py" in globals()
    and "cpr_model_py" in globals()
    and "zip_result_py" in globals()
    and "testing_data" in globals()
):
    from scipy.special import gammaln

    zip_alt_covariates_py = [
        "driver_age",
        "annual_mileage",
        "vehicle_age",
        "male",
        "urban_area",
        "prior_claims",
    ]

    zip_alt_testing_py = testing_data.copy()
    for col in zip_alt_covariates_py + ["claims"]:
        zip_alt_testing_py[col] = pd.to_numeric(
            zip_alt_testing_py[col],
            errors="coerce",
        )

    X_alt_test_py = sm.add_constant(
        zip_alt_testing_py[zip_alt_covariates_py].astype(float),
        has_constant="add",
    )

    lr_test_p_claim_py = np.asarray(
        lr_model_py.predict(X_alt_test_py),
        dtype=float,
    )
    lr_test_p_zero_py = 1 - lr_test_p_claim_py

    cpr_test_mu_py = np.asarray(
        cpr_model_py.predict(X_alt_test_py),
        dtype=float,
    )
    cpr_test_p_zero_py = np.exp(-cpr_test_mu_py)

    zip_alt_testing_py["driver_age_10"] = (
        zip_alt_testing_py["driver_age"] / 10
    )
    zip_alt_testing_py["annual_mileage_10k"] = (
        zip_alt_testing_py["annual_mileage"] / 10000
    )
    zip_alt_testing_py["vehicle_age_5"] = (
        zip_alt_testing_py["vehicle_age"] / 5
    )

    zip_alt_scaled_covariates_py = [
        "driver_age_10",
        "annual_mileage_10k",
        "vehicle_age_5",
        "male",
        "urban_area",
        "prior_claims",
    ]

    X_zip_alt_test_py = sm.add_constant(
        zip_alt_testing_py[zip_alt_scaled_covariates_py].astype(float),
        has_constant="add",
    )

    zip_test_mu_py = np.asarray(
        zip_result_py.predict(
            exog=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            exog_infl=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            which="mean",
        ),
        dtype=float,
    )
    zip_test_lambda_py = np.asarray(
        zip_result_py.predict(
            exog=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            exog_infl=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            which="mean-main",
        ),
        dtype=float,
    )
    zip_test_pi_py = 1 - np.asarray(
        zip_result_py.predict(
            exog=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            exog_infl=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            which="prob-main",
        ),
        dtype=float,
    )
    zip_test_p_zero_py = np.asarray(
        zip_result_py.predict(
            exog=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            exog_infl=X_zip_alt_test_py,
            which="prob-zero",
        ),
        dtype=float,
    )

    claims_test_py = zip_alt_testing_py["claims"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    observed_zero_test_py = (claims_test_py == 0).astype(int)

    def zip_alt_point_metric_row_py(model_name, prediction):
        prediction = np.asarray(prediction, dtype=float)
        error = claims_test_py - prediction
        return {
            "model": model_name,
            "mean_error": np.mean(error),
            "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(error)),
            "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean(error ** 2)),
        }

    point_rows_py = [
        zip_alt_point_metric_row_py(
            "Classical Poisson Regression",
            cpr_test_mu_py,
        ),
        zip_alt_point_metric_row_py(
            "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression",
            zip_test_mu_py,
        ),
    ]
    zip_alt_point_metrics_py = pd.DataFrame(point_rows_py)

    def zip_alt_zero_metric_row_py(model_name, predicted_p_zero):
        p = np.clip(
            np.asarray(predicted_p_zero, dtype=float),
            1e-12,
            1 - 1e-12,
        )
        return {
            "model": model_name,
            "zero_brier_score": np.mean(
                (observed_zero_test_py - p) ** 2
            ),
            "zero_log_loss": -np.mean(
                observed_zero_test_py * np.log(p)
                + (1 - observed_zero_test_py) * np.log(1 - p)
            ),
        }

    zero_rows_py = [
        zip_alt_zero_metric_row_py(
            "Binary Logistic Regression",
            lr_test_p_zero_py,
        ),
        zip_alt_zero_metric_row_py(
            "Classical Poisson Regression",
            cpr_test_p_zero_py,
        ),
        zip_alt_zero_metric_row_py(
            "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression",
            zip_test_p_zero_py,
        ),
    ]
    zip_alt_zero_metrics_py = pd.DataFrame(zero_rows_py)

    cpr_log_mass_py = (
        -cpr_test_mu_py
        + claims_test_py * np.log(np.clip(cpr_test_mu_py, 1e-12, None))
        - gammaln(claims_test_py + 1)
    )

    zip_positive_log_mass_py = (
        np.log(np.clip(1 - zip_test_pi_py, 1e-12, None))
        - zip_test_lambda_py
        + claims_test_py * np.log(
            np.clip(zip_test_lambda_py, 1e-12, None)
        )
        - gammaln(claims_test_py + 1)
    )
    zip_log_mass_py = np.where(
        claims_test_py == 0,
        np.log(np.clip(zip_test_p_zero_py, 1e-12, None)),
        zip_positive_log_mass_py,
    )

    zip_alt_distribution_metrics_py = pd.DataFrame({
        "model": [
            "Classical Poisson Regression",
            "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression",
        ],
        "mean_negative_log_predictive_mass": [
            np.mean(-cpr_log_mass_py),
            np.mean(-zip_log_mass_py),
        ],
    })

    zip_alt_prediction_metrics_py = pd.DataFrame({
        "model": [
            "Binary Logistic Regression",
            "Classical Poisson Regression",
            "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression",
        ]
    })
    zip_alt_prediction_metrics_py = zip_alt_prediction_metrics_py.merge(
        zip_alt_point_metrics_py,
        on="model",
        how="left",
    ).merge(
        zip_alt_zero_metrics_py,
        on="model",
        how="left",
    ).merge(
        zip_alt_distribution_metrics_py,
        on="model",
        how="left",
    )

    metric_labels_py = {
        "mean_error": "Mean Error",
        "MAE": "MAE",
        "RMSE": "RMSE",
        "zero_brier_score": "Zero Brier Score",
        "zero_log_loss": "Zero Log Loss",
        "mean_negative_log_predictive_mass":
            "Mean Negative Log Predictive Mass",
    }

    zip_alt_prediction_plot_py = zip_alt_prediction_metrics_py.melt(
        id_vars="model",
        var_name="metric",
        value_name="value",
    ).dropna(subset=["value"])
    zip_alt_prediction_plot_py["metric"] = (
        zip_alt_prediction_plot_py["metric"]
        .map(metric_labels_py)
    )
```


:::

The blank LR cells are intentional. They are not missing results that need to be imputed. LR predicts the probability of crossing the zero-versus-positive boundary, but it does not specify how probability should be divided among one, two, three, or more claims. Consequently, it cannot be assigned a count-scale MAE/RMSE or an exact-count predictive-mass score without adding another model or an additional assumption.

For Mean Error, values closer to zero indicate less average signed bias. For MAE, RMSE, zero Brier score, zero log loss, and mean negative log predictive mass, smaller values indicate better held-out performance.

For **held-out expected-count prediction**, CPR and ZIP are both almost unbiased on average. CPR's Mean Error, **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$mean_error[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"])`**, is slightly closer to zero than ZIP's **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$mean_error[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"])`**, but both values are tiny relative to the claim-count scale. ZIP performs better on the unsigned error measures: its MAE is **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$MAE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"])`** claims compared with **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$MAE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"])`** for CPR, and its RMSE is **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$RMSE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"])`** compared with **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$RMSE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"])`**. These are improvements of only about **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (1 - zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$MAE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"] / zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$MAE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"]))`%** in MAE and **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (1 - zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$RMSE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"] / zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$RMSE[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"]))`%** in RMSE, so the policyholder-specific point-prediction advantage is real but modest.

For the shared **observed-zero probability** target, ZIP is narrowly best on the held-out data, but LR remains essentially tied. The ZIP Brier score is **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$zero_brier_score[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"])`**, compared with **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$zero_brier_score[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Binary Logistic Regression"])`** for LR; the corresponding zero-event log losses are **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$zero_log_loss[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"])`** and **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$zero_log_loss[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Binary Logistic Regression"])`**. Those differences are extremely small. CPR is substantially worse on both zero-event scores. Thus, ZIP preserves the strong occurrence prediction of the dedicated binary model while also modelling the positive-count distribution, but LR remains highly competitive if zero versus positive is the only predictive question.

For the **complete held-out count distribution**, the separation between the two count models is much larger. ZIP has mean negative log predictive mass **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$mean_negative_log_predictive_mass[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"])`**, compared with **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$mean_negative_log_predictive_mass[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"])`** for CPR. This is a reduction of about **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (1 - zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$mean_negative_log_predictive_mass[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression"] / zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$mean_negative_log_predictive_mass[zip_alt_prediction_metrics_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"]))`%**. The ZIP distribution therefore assigns appreciably more probability, on average, to the exact held-out claim counts that are observed. LR has no corresponding complete-count score because it does not specify probabilities for one, two, three, or more claims.

The panel-wise rankings in @fig-zip-alternatives-prediction-metrics-r and @fig-zip-alternatives-prediction-metrics-py match the numerical conclusions above. CPR's Mean Error bar lies slightly closer to zero, whereas ZIP has the lower MAE and RMSE. On the two zero-event panels, LR and ZIP are visually almost indistinguishable and both outperform CPR, with ZIP narrowly lower on the held-out scores. The largest visual separation between the two count models appears in mean negative log predictive mass, where ZIP is clearly lower than CPR. The missing LR bars for Mean Error, MAE, RMSE, and mean negative log predictive mass are intentional rather than missing data: Binary Logistic Regression does not define a marginal claim-count prediction or a complete predictive distribution over the count values.

### What do the comparisons tell us jointly?

No single statistic answers every question in this section. A model can be attractive inferentially because its parameters answer a useful scientific question, yet still have weak residual behaviour or little held-out predictive advantage. Conversely, a simpler model may predict one observable target well while deliberately ignoring other features of the response.

The final comparison should therefore combine **model scope, fitted adequacy, residual diagnostics, predictive performance, and complexity**.

| **Comparison dimension** | **Binary Logistic Regression** | **Classical Poisson Regression** | **Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression** | **Joint conclusion** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Inferential target | Odds of at least one observed claim | Expected claim count under one Poisson process | Structural-zero odds and count-state expected claims | Different estimands; do not rank by number of significant coefficients |
| Count-response AIC/BIC | Not comparable because the response is `has_claim` | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-count-fit-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-count-fit-r | ZIP is strongly favoured over CPR: CPR is **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_count_fit_r$delta_AIC[zip_alt_count_fit_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"])`** AIC points and **`r fmt_sig(zip_alt_count_fit_r$delta_BIC[zip_alt_count_fit_r$model == "Classical Poisson Regression"])`** BIC points above ZIP despite ZIP's additional parameters. |
| Common zero-event fitted quality | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-zero-fit-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-zero-fit-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-zero-fit-r | LR is marginally best in sample; ZIP is essentially tied with LR, while CPR is clearly worse at representing observed zeros. |
| Residual adequacy | See @fig-zip-alternatives-residuals-r | See @fig-zip-alternatives-residuals-r | See @fig-zip-alternatives-residuals-r | CPR leaves the strongest count-scale residual spread and drift. ZIP substantially reduces that structure; LR is broadly adequate for its separate binary target. |
| Held-out expected-count accuracy | Not defined by LR | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | CPR has Mean Error slightly closer to zero, but ZIP has modestly lower MAE and RMSE. |
| Held-out zero-event probability | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | ZIP is narrowly best on Brier score and log loss; LR is effectively tied, while CPR is clearly worse. |
| Held-out complete count distribution | Not defined by LR | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | See @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r | ZIP assigns substantially more probability to the exact held-out counts than CPR, as shown by its lower mean negative log predictive mass. |
| Complexity and interpretability | Simplest; one binary mechanism | Simple count model; one mean mechanism | Most flexible; two linked mechanisms and more parameters | ZIP's extra flexibility is worthwhile for the full count problem in this dataset, but LR remains the more parsimonious choice when the only target is claim occurrence. |

: Joint comparison framework for Binary Logistic, Classical Poisson, and Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression. {#tbl-zip-alternatives-joint-findings .striped .hover}

Taken together, the comparisons support the added ZIP mechanism when the objective is to model the **full claim-count response**. Relative to Classical Poisson Regression, ZIP improves the training likelihood enough to remain strongly favoured after both AIC and BIC penalize its seven additional parameters. The calibration and residual diagnostics explain why: CPR systematically assigns too little probability to observed zeros and leaves substantially greater Pearson-residual spread and fitted-value drift, whereas ZIP captures the zero mass separately and produces a more stable count-scale residual pattern. The improvement is therefore not merely an information-criterion artifact; it corresponds to the empirical feature that motivated the model in the first place.

The predictive comparison is more nuanced. For held-out expected counts, ZIP has lower MAE and RMSE than CPR, but the improvement is modest and CPR's Mean Error is actually slightly closer to zero. The largest count-model predictive gain appears when the **complete distribution** is evaluated: ZIP has a clearly lower mean negative log predictive mass, so it assigns more probability on average to the exact held-out counts. On the common zero-versus-positive target, the dedicated Binary Logistic Regression model remains highly competitive. LR is marginally better than ZIP on the training zero-event scores, while ZIP is only narrowly better on the held-out Brier score and log loss. Consequently, the extra ZIP structure is not needed simply to obtain a strong binary prediction of whether any claim occurs.

For this synthetic dataset, ZIP is therefore the most informative choice when the analysis requires the complete count distribution and a substantively meaningful separation between structural-zero membership and count-state claim frequency. CPR is more parsimonious but does not represent the zero-heavy count distribution nearly as well. LR remains preferable when the scientific or operational question is genuinely limited to **claim versus no claim**, because it achieves essentially the same zero-event predictive quality with a simpler estimand and fewer modelling assumptions. The model comparison therefore supports ZIP for the chapter's full count-data inquiry without implying that greater flexibility should always be preferred regardless of the target.

The comparison should not be read as a rule that ZIP must win because the data contain many zeros. LR may remain the most direct model when the practical question is only whether **any** claim occurs. CPR may remain preferable when a one-process count model is adequate and interpretability or parsimony is a priority. ZIP becomes most compelling when the data and the substantive problem both support a distinct zero-generating mechanism **and** the additional flexibility leads to better fitted adequacy, more useful inference, or stronger held-out prediction.

Because this running example uses synthetic insurance data, the final ranking demonstrates how to compare regression approaches rather than establishing a general result about insurance claims. In an applied analysis, model choice should also consider the scientific plausibility of the latent structural-zero state, the stability of the estimated ZIP components, and whether the additional complexity changes decisions that matter to the analysis.


## Storytelling {#sec-zip-storytelling}

The last stage of a regression analysis is not another coefficient table or diagnostic plot. It is the task of explaining **what the evidence says about the original inquiry**, why the chosen model is useful, and which conclusions would go beyond what the data can support. In our synthetic insurance-claims example, we have compared three approaches that answer related but different questions: Binary Logistic Regression (LR) describes **whether any claim was observed**, Classical Poisson Regression (CPR) describes **claim counts through one Poisson process**, and Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression (ZIP) allows **two latent routes to an observed zero** while retaining a complete probability distribution for nonnegative counts.

The study design in @sec-zip-study-design established two inquiries. The **inferential inquiry** concerns how policyholder and vehicle characteristics are associated with the ZIP structural-zero probability, count-state mean, and marginal expected count. The **predictive inquiry** concerns the accuracy of the training-fitted model when predicting the claims of policyholders held out from estimation. A responsible final story must address both, without treating coefficient significance as predictive success or predictive accuracy as proof of a structural mechanism.

### A briefing for an insurance analytics team {#sec-zip-storytelling-briefing}

Imagine that an insurance analytics team asks: *What have we learned about the drivers of claim frequency, and does the additional ZIP structure actually help us describe and predict claims?* The evidence can be organised into the short briefing in @tbl-zip-storytelling-briefing.

| **Stakeholder question** | **Evidence used in this chapter** | **Practical interpretation** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Which characteristics show the clearest adjusted associations? | The frozen-specification testing-set refit and the component and joint Wald results in @sec-zip-parameter-inference. | Annual mileage and the prior-claims indicator provide the clearest and comparatively stable model-based associations. In this example, both are associated with *lower structural-zero odds* and *higher expected claims within the count-generating state*. Other effects require more caution, especially where intervals are wide or conclusions change near a conventional threshold. |
| Does ZIP explain why the observed zeros are difficult for CPR? | The training zero-probability calibration in @fig-zip-alternatives-zero-calibration-r and the count-model diagnostics in @sec-zip-goodness-of-fit. | Across the fitted-probability groups, CPR tends to assign too little probability to no-claim outcomes. ZIP substantially improves the description of this observed feature; the two-component formulation is therefore responding to an actual diagnostic problem rather than merely adding parameters. |
| Does the more flexible model also improve residual behaviour? | The training Pearson-residual comparison in @fig-zip-alternatives-residuals-r. | CPR leaves more pronounced count-scale residual spread and fitted-value drift. ZIP reduces these patterns, although its residuals are not perfectly pattern-free. LR residuals concern a **binary** response and cannot be ranked on exactly the same numerical scale as count-model residuals. |
| Does ZIP improve held-out prediction? | The training-fitted models scored on the testing data in @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r. | ZIP yields modestly smaller MAE and RMSE for expected counts, markedly better complete-count predictive mass than CPR, and substantially better zero-event probability scores than CPR. LR remains essentially competitive with ZIP when the only question is whether any claim occurs. |
| Should we treat ZIP's latent classifications as known insurance facts? | The modelling assumptions in @sec-zip-study-design and @sec-zip-goodness-of-fit. | No. The structural-zero state is **latent**. An observed zero could also come from the Poisson count state. The synthetic dataset does not establish which state generated any one policyholder's zero or validate a real-world explanation of structural ineligibility. |

: Stakeholder-facing synthesis of the inferential and predictive ZIP inquiries in the synthetic insurance-claims example. {#tbl-zip-storytelling-briefing .striped .hover}

The key finding is not simply that the most elaborate model wins. Rather, **the model choice depends on the quantity we need to learn or predict**. If the team only needs a probability that a policyholder files at least one claim, the simpler LR model already addresses that question directly and performs similarly to ZIP on the zero-versus-positive target. If the team needs the expected **number** of claims and the probabilities of particular claim counts, LR leaves important aspects of the response undefined. ZIP is more informative for that fuller task because it models both the zero mass and the distribution of positive count outcomes.

### Why the graphical comparison matters {#sec-zip-storytelling-visual-evidence}

The zero-calibration panels in @fig-zip-alternatives-zero-calibration-r make the motivation for ZIP visible to readers without requiring them to interpret its likelihood equations. The fitted CPR model repeatedly assigns **less** probability to zero claims than the observed group frequencies suggest. By contrast, ZIP and LR are closer to the observed zero frequencies, with no comparable persistent one-direction discrepancy. This is exactly the feature the additional ZIP mechanism was introduced to accommodate. Nevertheless, LR's success on this graph should not be surprising: it was fitted specifically to a binary claim-versus-no-claim outcome. Good zero calibration is necessary for a zero-heavy count model, but it does not on its own demonstrate that the **entire** count distribution is adequate.

The residual panels in @fig-zip-alternatives-residuals-r provide a complementary perspective. CPR's larger standardized residual spread and stronger fitted-value trend suggest that the one-process Poisson formulation is missing structure in the claim counts. ZIP reduces that structure by separating the zero probability from the count-state mean. This does not mean that ZIP solves every lack-of-fit problem, nor that a Pearson-residual plot can identify which individual zeros are structural. Also, the LR panel is calculated for `has_claim`, while the CPR and ZIP panels are calculated for `claims`; it is therefore the **within-panel patterns**, rather than direct comparison of the LR and count residual magnitudes, that are informative.

Finally, the held-out results in @tbl-zip-alternatives-prediction-r explain why **a visually much better model of zero claims does not necessarily produce a dramatically smaller RMSE**. RMSE evaluates the differences between observed counts $Y_i$ and the **predicted marginal expected counts** $\widehat{\mu}_i$; it does not evaluate the probability assigned to $Y_i=0$ or to each exact count. CPR and ZIP can generate fairly similar $\widehat{\mu}_i$ even while assigning very different probability masses to the possible outcomes. Moreover, occasional larger counts contribute disproportionately to squared error, and no count model can remove the chance variability in realised claims. ZIP's advantage here is therefore **more pronounced in describing and forecasting the count distribution** than in reducing the squared error of its point predictions. A similar RMSE is not evidence that the two likelihood models are equivalent.

### A concise stakeholder message {#sec-zip-storytelling-message}

> *In this synthetic insurance-claims example, policyholder mileage and prior-claims history show the most consistent adjusted associations with the fitted claim processes. A standard Poisson model struggles to reproduce the observed frequency of no-claim policyholders and leaves more systematic residual structure. The ZIP model handles those features better and assigns more probability to the observed held-out claim counts, although its improvement in expected-count RMSE is modest. If our only task were predicting claim versus no claim, a simpler Logistic model would remain a strong alternative. The two-state explanation should be treated as a useful modelling assumption—not proof that individual policyholders belong to an identifiable structural-zero group.*

This message answers the two inquiries without overstating either. The **inferential conclusion** concerns adjusted associations in a fitted synthetic-data model, including uncertainty and stability; it is not a causal account of insurance risk. The **predictive conclusion** concerns held-out performance of the model estimated on the training data, not the refitted testing-set model. The same testing outcomes also appear in the split-sample inferential comparison, so the two assessments should not be advertised as independent external validations. The next section considers when this type of model, and these conclusions, may be unreliable in practice.

## Practical Considerations {#sec-zip-practical-considerations}

ZIP regression is a useful extension of the count-regression toolkit, but it is **not a one-size-fits-all response to a high proportion of zeros**. A fitted ZIP model can reproduce the observed count distribution while providing weak information about its latent components, or it can fit one dataset well without generalising to another. Practical model choice must therefore account for the substantive meaning of zero, the distribution of positive counts, the available information, the dependence structure, and the eventual use of the predictions [@lambert1992zip; @cameron2013countdata].

### Excess observed zeros do not establish a separate zero-generating state {#sec-zip-practical-zero-mechanism}

ZIP assumes that an observation may come from a **structural-zero state** with probability $\pi_i$, or from a **Poisson count state** with probability $1-\pi_i$. The second state can itself produce zero. Consequently, the probability of an observed zero is

$$
\Pr(Y_i=0\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)\exp(-\lambda_i).
$$

This expression is useful for prediction, but its two terms are **not separately observed labels**. In the insurance setting, a policyholder with no recorded claim is not automatically in a group that could not have filed a claim. They may simply have experienced no claim during the observation period. A plausible structural mechanism would require information about the policy, coverage, exposure, and reporting process that is not available in this synthetic example.

An unusually large number of zeros can arise without a distinct zero state: unmeasured differences in exposure, omitted regressors, heterogeneous claim rates, a misspecified relationship with the regressors, or a different count distribution can all change the expected zero frequency. Thus, a favourable ZIP AIC or calibration plot **supports the usefulness of a fitted distribution**, but does not by itself establish a physical or behavioural zero-generating mechanism. When the existence of two states is the main scientific claim, substantive evidence outside the regression fit is essential.

### Overdispersion and choosing another count model {#sec-zip-practical-dispersion}

ZIP also changes the variance structure relative to Classical Poisson Regression. Writing the marginal mean as $\mu_i=(1-\pi_i)\lambda_i$, the ZIP conditional variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\mu_i+\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\lambda_i^2.
$$

The extra nonnegative term shows how the mixture can generate **overdispersion** even though the count-generating state remains Poisson. However, this does **not** mean that a ZIP model accommodates every source of excess variance. If the positive counts are more variable than a Poisson distribution permits, even after accounting for zeros and regressors, a different count distribution or model structure may be necessary. Likewise, a Negative Binomial model can sometimes accommodate both the larger variance and many of the zeros *without* invoking a separate structural-zero group.

@tbl-zip-practical-model-choices places the main alternatives in the context of the problem they address.

| **Model** | **Main modelling feature** | **When it deserves consideration** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Classical Poisson Regression (@sec-classical-poisson) | One count-generating process; conditional variance equals conditional mean. | The observed counts and fitted zero probabilities are reasonably compatible with the Poisson formulation. |
| Negative Binomial Regression (@sec-negative-binomial) | A more flexible count variance than Classical Poisson Regression. | Overdispersion persists, potentially explaining numerous zeros without a separate zero-generating state. |
| Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression | A latent zero-only state plus a Poisson count state. | A separate zero-producing mechanism is substantively defensible, and the model improves the relevant diagnostics or prediction targets. |
| Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Regression | A latent zero-only state plus an overdispersed Negative Binomial count state. | Both a distinct zero mechanism and additional count-state variation appear relevant; the increased parameter burden is supportable. |
| Hurdle model | A separate process for zero versus positive, followed by a **zero-truncated** count distribution for positive outcomes. | The main distinction is **whether any event occurs** versus **how many occur after the hurdle has been crossed**; unlike ZIP, the positive-count component cannot generate zeros. |
| Generalized Poisson Regression (@sec-generalized-poisson) | An alternative count distribution with a more flexible mean–variance relationship. | The principal concern is count dispersion rather than evidence for a latent zero-only state. |

: Choosing among count models according to the substantive mechanism and remaining distributional misfit. {#tbl-zip-practical-model-choices .striped .hover}

A **hurdle model** is a particularly useful next concept. ZIP combines structural zeros with *ordinary Poisson sampling zeros*, whereas a hurdle formulation puts all observed zeros on one side of the hurdle and uses a zero-truncated distribution on the positive side. This distinction changes the interpretation of each component: a hurdle model describes the probability of crossing the observed zero-versus-positive boundary; ZIP introduces an **unobserved** structural-zero state. Neither parameterisation should be chosen simply because its name seems to match a high zero rate [@hu2011zeroinflatedhurdle; @cameron2013countdata].

### Limited data and the cost of modelling two components {#sec-zip-practical-sample-size}

Every ZIP fit estimates **two linked regression components**. When the same six regressors and an intercept are included in each component, the model has fourteen regression coefficients rather than the seven of a comparable Classical Poisson model. This additional flexibility may improve the fit, but it also requires the data to distinguish a change in $\pi_i$ from a change in $\lambda_i$. A large overall sample is not enough if most of the observations provide little information about one of those components.

In particular, **very few positive counts**, sparse binary-regressor categories, near-deterministic zero/nonzero patterns, or limited overlap between regressor groups can make the zero-state coefficients weakly identified. The numerical optimiser may converge despite large estimates, unstable curvature, inflated standard errors, or wide confidence intervals. The inverse-Hessian covariance matrix is only as trustworthy as the local identification and large-sample approximation that justify it. Strong conclusions should not be drawn from a coefficient merely because software prints a finite estimate or a small $p$-value.

This matters for the current study design because the testing-set refit contains substantially fewer observations than the training fit. It is intended to illustrate coefficient stability under a frozen specification, not to make uncertainty disappear. With limited data, analysts should consider a more parsimonious zero component, prespecified covariate selection, sensitivity analyses, bootstrap uncertainty where computationally feasible, or scientifically justified regularisation. There is no universal minimum number of observations or zero counts that guarantees reliable ZIP inference.

### Multicollinearity and competing explanations {#sec-zip-practical-multicollinearity}

ZIP is especially vulnerable to **interpretive overreach when regressors overlap in the information they contain**. For example, annual mileage, an urban-driving indicator, and past claims could all be associated with exposure or driving behaviour. When regressors are strongly correlated, the model has less information to separate their *adjusted* associations. Coefficients may become sensitive to adding or removing other variables, confidence intervals may widen, and it may become difficult to say which characteristic contributes independently.

This is a problem of **precision, stability, and attribution**, not proof that the coefficients are inherently biased or that all correlated regressors must be removed. Exact linear dependence prevents unique estimation; high but imperfect correlation does not automatically invalidate a fitted model. In ZIP, there are also two sources of potential difficulty: collinearity **within** each component's design matrix and competition **between** the zero and count components for explaining the observed frequency of zeros. They are related modelling concerns but are not the same phenomenon.

Useful checks include examining covariate correlations and category frequencies, inspecting the rank and condition of both component design matrices, considering variance inflation factors where appropriate, examining the stability of the joint covariance matrix, and checking whether substantive conclusions persist under defensible alternative specifications. Any simplification should preserve the study's inferential question rather than dropping variables solely to obtain smaller $p$-values. Fitted marginal quantities and policyholder-profile contrasts can be easier to communicate than a long list of unstable component coefficients.

### Exposure, dependence, and specification {#sec-zip-practical-design}

The observation window and exposure definition matter for count outcomes. Two policyholders observed for different lengths of time or under different coverage conditions should not automatically be treated as having equal claim opportunities. When it is scientifically appropriate to model **rates**, a known exposure measure can enter the count-component log link as an **offset**. Whether exposure also helps describe structural-zero membership is a separate substantive question. A missing or incorrect exposure definition can produce apparent zero inflation and misleading regression coefficients.

The simple ZIP model developed in this chapter also assumes that policyholder responses are conditionally independent and that the logit and log-link systematic components provide adequate descriptions of their respective relationships. Repeated observations for the same policyholder, clustering by location or insurer, unmodelled nonlinearities, interactions, influential counts, or omitted heterogeneity can violate these simplifications. Depending on the data, useful extensions include mixed-effects or hierarchical count models, richer functional forms, and alternative count distributions. In all cases, the more elaborate model should answer a documented deficiency rather than merely provide a lower in-sample information criterion.

### Distinguishing different kinds of model evidence {#sec-zip-practical-evidence}

The chapter has used several forms of evidence, each with a different role:

- **Inferential quantities**—component coefficients, Wald tests, confidence intervals, joint coefficient tests, and marginal scenario contrasts—describe model-based associations and their uncertainty under the assumed specification.
- **Training-stage diagnostics**—observed-versus-fitted zero frequencies, calibration, residual patterns, and comparisons of observed and fitted counts—show whether the fitted model captures important empirical features used during development.
- **Information criteria**—AIC and BIC for models fitted to the *same count response*—balance in-sample likelihood with a penalty for complexity. They are not proofs that a latent mechanism exists.
- **Held-out predictive metrics**—RMSE, MAE, zero-event Brier score and log loss, and mean negative log predictive mass—measure different targets and may therefore rank models differently. Model choice should follow the target rather than an arbitrary winning metric.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on tests of the zero-inflation mechanism!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
A **joint test of the zero-inflation slopes** within a fitted ZIP model asks whether the observed regressors contribute to its latent zero-state probability *beyond a constant zero-state probability*. This is distinct from testing whether a zero-inflation component is needed at all. Under the null hypothesis of **no zero inflation**, $\pi_i=0$ for every policyholder; with a logit zero component, that null is approached as its intercept tends toward $-\infty$, and its slopes are not identified in the usual way. Therefore, the familiar interior-parameter Chi-squared reference distribution for an ordinary likelihood-ratio test is generally **not justified** for the full CPR-versus-ZIP comparison.

Specialised score tests for extra zeros, including the approach of [van den Broek (1995)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2532959) and its covariate-dependent extensions, or a carefully designed **parametric-bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison**, are possible approaches. Their assumptions and null distributions must be checked for the actual fitted specification. In particular, an ordinary non-nested Vuong test should **not** be used uncritically as an omnibus test of zero inflation. For this teaching example, AIC/BIC, calibration, residual evidence, and held-out predictions are the main reported comparisons; we do **not** claim that these are a formal boundary-corrected hypothesis test of $\pi_i=0$.
::::
:::

### Responsibility when reporting results {#sec-zip-practical-responsibility}

Even when ZIP gives a good fitted description of claims, the results remain **model-based associations**. Observational regressors are not treatments assigned at random; a coefficient does not identify the effect of changing a policyholder's mileage, moving a driver between urban and rural settings, or altering prior-claims history. In an actual insurance application, questions of measurement quality, differences across portfolios and time, privacy, fairness, and the consequences of deploying model-based decisions would also require attention. The synthetic dataset in this chapter is valuable for demonstrating methodology, but it cannot establish reliable risk estimates or policy recommendations for real customers.

Finally, no diagnostic certifies that a model will remain adequate indefinitely. A model intended for operational use would require data collected under a clearly documented design, external or temporal validation, monitoring of zero frequencies and count distributions, and review when conditions change. The best model is the **simplest defensible model that answers the inferential or predictive question adequately**, not necessarily the model with the most terms.

## Chapter Summary {#sec-chapter-12-summary}

This chapter introduced **Zero-Inflated Poisson (ZIP) Regression** as a model for nonnegative integer counts in which more than one mechanism may produce observed zeros. We began with a synthetic insurance-claims dataset, compared Binary Logistic and Classical Poisson Regression, and developed ZIP as a model combining a **latent zero-only state** with an **ordinary Poisson count state**. The central idea was not that every zero is structural; it was that a zero can arise from either part of the mixture.

For policyholder $i$, the fitted ZIP model distinguishes the structural-zero probability $\pi_i$, the count-state Poisson mean $\lambda_i$, and the marginal expected count $\mu_i$. Their relationship is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_i=0\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
&=\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)e^{-\lambda_i},\\[4pt]
\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
&=\mu_i=(1-\pi_i)\lambda_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Two regression components connect the observed regressors with $\pi_i$ through a logit link and with $\lambda_i$ through a log link. Their coefficients consequently have **different interpretations**: exponentiated zero-component coefficients represent odds ratios for latent structural-zero membership, while exponentiated count-component coefficients represent rate ratios for the Poisson count-state mean. Neither coefficient block alone generally determines the regressor's association with the **marginal expected claim count**. Scenario-based quantities and their uncertainty are useful for communicating their combined implications.

We organised the empirical work around the two inquiries in @tbl-zip-chapter-summary-inquiries.

| **Inquiry** | **Question answered** | **Main lesson from the synthetic example** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Inferential** | How are policyholder and vehicle regressors associated with structural-zero membership, count-state claim frequency, and marginal expected claims? | Annual mileage and prior-claims history show the clearest and most stable adjusted associations across the two components. Other patterns are less precise, and component-specific associations should not be mistaken for marginal or causal effects. |
| **Predictive** | How well does a training-fitted model predict observed zero probabilities, expected counts, and the full count distribution for held-out policyholders? | ZIP improves substantially on CPR for the observed-zero probability and exact-count predictive mass, but produces only a modest improvement in count-scale MAE and RMSE. A simpler LR model is highly competitive for zero-versus-positive prediction alone. |

: Summary of the inferential and predictive inquiries in the synthetic insurance-claims study. {#tbl-zip-chapter-summary-inquiries .striped .hover}

The workflow also illustrated that **estimation, inference, model assessment, and prediction are separate activities**. We first examined the response and regressors in the training data, fitted ZIP by maximising its joint likelihood, and evaluated numerical completion and model adequacy. The frozen specification was then refitted on the testing observations for a split-sample inferential comparison, while the *original training fit* was used unchanged to generate held-out predictions. The resulting testing-set coefficient intervals and tests do not have the same purpose as the held-out predictive scores, and the shared testing outcomes do not create two independent external validations.

Most importantly, the comparison with simpler models taught us to **match the model to the question**. The training zero-calibration and Pearson-residual plots show why Classical Poisson Regression can struggle with a zero-heavy count distribution. ZIP's additional mechanism reduces this lack of fit and supports a better model of complete claim-count probabilities. Nevertheless, a model can improve distributional fit without greatly improving RMSE, because the fitted mean and the full predictive distribution answer different questions. Similarly, a simple Binary Logistic model can predict the occurrence of *any* claim well without modelling the number of claims.

ZIP is therefore a **valuable model, not a universal prescription**. Before using it, analysts should examine whether a separate zero-only mechanism is scientifically credible, whether the count state is still overdispersed, whether the observations and regressors contain enough information to estimate both components reliably, and whether multicollinearity, exposure differences, dependence, or misspecification weaken the conclusions. Negative Binomial, zero-inflated Negative Binomial, hurdle, and generalized count models each address somewhat different shortcomings, and may be more appropriate for a given response [@hu2011zeroinflatedhurdle; @cameron2013countdata].

The main takeaway of this chapter is methodological: **a useful regression analysis is not defined by the number of significant coefficients or by one model-selection statistic**. It begins with a clear inferential or predictive inquiry, follows the evidence from the fitted data and diagnostics, makes comparisons on compatible targets, and ends with an explanation of what the model can and cannot establish. The synthetic insurance example provides a complete introduction to that workflow for counts with excess zeros, while leaving more flexible discrete-response and hurdle models as natural extensions.
